concept_systems.concept_name: The Cat Model (systems-first concept for Cat As Rophe)
concept_systems.one_line_pitch: An insurance company's catastrophe simulation takes its own jargon literally and spawns the "cat event" as an actual cat: you are Rophe, the catastrophe itself, loose in a table-top city where every man-made thing burns, floods, shorts, corrodes, melts and buckles by rule, and the more you destroy, the greener the world gets.
concept_systems.style_answer:
VERDICT: neither pixel art nor a block world. Build a 3D HYBRID: real-model mesh fracture for everything man-made, a smooth voxel ground, and an invisible coarse cell grid that carries the rules. Keep the pixel-sandbox SOUL (every material reacts with every other), drop the pixel-sandbox LOOK.

The three options, judged against this brief:
- 2D falling-sand game. Unbeatable for "every pixel reacts", but it cannot be this game: no open 3D world (req. 1), no climbing (5), no real 3D models (8), no cat's-eye spectacle (9).
- Full 3D voxel world. One uniform rule set, but at a voxel small enough to look good (0.25 m) this map is about 21 billion cells, far beyond what GDScript can mesh or simulate; at an affordable 1 m it looks like toy blocks, which kills the AAA feel and makes requirement 8 pointless. The old prototype's 1.5 m boxes were exactly this failure.
- Hybrid (chosen). Three layers, each doing only what it is best at:
  A. THINGS (the looks). Buildings, vehicles and props are real models from modular free kits, cut offline by a Python pipeline into structural elements (columns, beams, slabs, wall panels, glazing), each pre-fractured into 6-40 shards with material-specific inner faces.
  B. GROUND (the digging). Smooth voxel terrain at 0.5 m with 12 strata materials, stored as "procedural column + sparse edits". Roads and pavements are rigid fracture plates lying on top of it, because thin crisp slabs are what voxels do worst.
  C. THE FIELD (the rules). A sparse 3D grid of 1 m cells around the player. Each cell holds a temperature, one fluid (water, fuel, acid, lava, milk), one gas (fuel gas, steam, smoke, dust) and an electric charge, and updates 10 times a second by local falling-sand rules. This IS the pixel sandbox, hidden inside the 3D world. Every Thing and every voxel carries one of 16 materials and reads from and writes to the Field.

The entire game is driven by one editable data table: 16 materials x 7 stimuli (impact, heat, water, electricity, acid, lava, pressure). If a reaction is in the table it works everywhere: on a wine glass, a tower column, a car door and a clay layer 8 m underground. That consistency is the "pixel sandbox" feeling, and it is also what lets a non-programmer director tune the game by editing a spreadsheet.

The pixel layer is not only hidden. MODEL VISION (one key) shows the Field as translucent false-colour cells: gas concentration, heat, water depth, live current, and the stress in every column. It is the game's "pixel sandbox mode", its planning tool and its simulation aesthetic at once.

LOOK: "scale-model realism" (see art direction): the city reads as an exquisitely lit architect's model on a table. The psychedelic streak of the first prototype survives in two places: Model Vision's false-colour palette and Catnip Frenzy.
concept_systems.story:
PREMISE. In the insurance industry "cat" is everyday shorthand for catastrophe: cat models, cat events, cat bonds. Solid Ground Mutual runs a huge "cat model": a simulated copy of the city of Port Indemnity, built for one purpose, to be destroyed over and over so the company can price its policies. One night an event is launched with PERIL TYPE: CAT and EVENT NAME: ROPHE, and the Model takes "cat" literally. Log line: ROPHE AS CAT. The catastrophe is instantiated as a small stray cat behind a bar in the old town. That is you.

THE TURN. The event was cast as a cat ("X as Y" is literally how code casts one type into another); then the cat takes over the event: CAT AS ROPHE. Rophe is not a prisoner of the simulation and not a villain. Rophe is the catastrophe this world was built to receive, with a cat's motive: things on tables must be knocked off them. The city turns out to be standing on one very large table.

WHY THIS FICTION: it explains seven otherwise arbitrary rules with one idea.
1. Cat hero and title pun: the "cat event" made flesh.
2. Everything man-made breaks: only insured property is in the Model's exposure database, so only it has a damage curve.
3. Nature and animals can never be harmed: nobody wrote a policy for the pigeons. No policy, no damage curve.
4. Rophe cannot die: the peril is not exposure either (and Rophe is an animal).
5. Humans can be harmed without gore: they are policyholders; when "lost" they fold into a stamped claim form.
6. Falling off the edge re-drops you somewhere random: an event that leaves the model domain is re-sampled at a random epicentre, which is what such models really do.
7. Rewind, freeze and replay are stolen scenario-runner controls; the score is insured loss in dollars; your rank is a "return period" (a 1-in-100-year cat, a 1-in-10,000-year cat).

THE DIRECTOR'S TWO IDEAS: keep both. The bar and the glowing treat stay as the inciting moment, but the treat is the Model's event token, not a drug: eating it binds the catastrophe to the cat. "The cat realises it lives in a simulation and tears it down" is the spine, but the realisation is PLAYED, not narrated: nobody tells the player; they find the edge. The psychedelic trip returns as Catnip Frenzy (catnip is the honest cat psychedelic).

ANTAGONIST. The Model itself, which speaks only in paperwork: asset tags, claim forms, news tickers and, as losses mount, PATCH NOTES ("v9.2: installed automatic gas shut-off valves. Known issue: cat."). Running joke: the Model never learns what ROPHE means, and every patch note tries a new expansion ("Rapid-Onset Property Hazard Event", "Really Obstinate Predator, Housecat-Equivalent"). No voice acting, no cutscene cast: all text, all cheap to make.

ARC. Act 1, Nuisance: a cat breaking glasses; the first edge discovery. Act 2, Named Event: districts fall, nature takes them back, the Model patches itself. Act 3, Total Loss: the insurer's tower falls, the Model tries to restore from backup, Rophe goes under the world and shreds the backups. Ending: the whole city is seen as a model on the Table; one prompt, one paw, it goes over the edge. Stinger: a real desk at night, a monitor reading MODEL DIVERGED - LOSS: INFINITE, a knocked-over mug, and a real cat asleep on the warm keyboard beside the event-name field holding the key-mash its paws typed: "rophe". A cat walking on a keyboard started all of it.

TONE. Slapstick bureaucracy versus a cat. Nothing is cruel: the humans are paperwork, the animals are untouchable, and destruction ends in a wild green valley rather than a wasteland.

FALLBACK if the insurance flavour does not land: the identical structure works as a city "disaster-drill twin" with the jargon removed. I recommend keeping it; it is the only version in which the title is the plot.
concept_systems.intro_sequence:
OPEN WITH AN INTRO: yes, but about 80 seconds long, of which only about 25 are non-interactive. Skippable at any moment by holding Esc / B for one second; plays automatically only when a new world is started; replayable from Extras. No dialogue, no narration, all in-engine. It explains nothing about simulations: that discovery belongs to the player.

0:00-0:07 TITLE GAG. Black screen, small monospace status line "[ INSTANTIATING EVENT... ]", then large: ROPHE AS CAT. Dot-matrix chatter. The line tears, the words swap through 0.6 s of false-colour static and land as the logo CAT AS ROPHE with a rubber-stamp thunk and a sub-bass purr. (This is the gag the prototype already has in C:\Users\Cayan\Desktop\CatAsRophe\scripts\intro.gd; it is kept, and now it means something.)
0:07-0:22 THE BAR. Rainy night in Old Quay. A camera at cat height follows a scruffy stray through a broken cellar window into The Ninth Life: warm light, six patrons, a bartender polishing glasses, an old dog asleep by the fire, a fern on the counter. The cat hops onto the bar and stops beside a full pint glass standing at the edge.
0:22-0:30 FIRST INPUT. The game waits. One prompt: [Swat]. The player pushes the glass off the counter. It shatters into real shards and the beer spills as real fluid. Bottom right, an adding-machine tape prints its first line: GLASSWARE, 1 - TOTAL LOSS - $4.00. The first verb the player learns is the game's thesis.
0:30-0:45 THE TREAT. One shard does not settle. It hovers, flickers into false colour, and a paper asset tag unfolds from it. Out of the spilled beer rises a glowing fish-shaped kibble: the event token. The cat sniffs it, bats it twice, eats it.
0:45-0:58 MODEL VISION. For five seconds the bar is shown as the Model sees it: contour lines of tiny ledger text crawl over every man-made surface; each patron carries a policy number; the bartender's tag reads LIFE - $250,000. The dog and the fern show nothing at all: full natural colour, no tag. (The nature rule, planted before the player can ask.)
0:58-1:20 HANDOVER. The bartender comes at you with a broom; prompt [Meow]. The meow blows out every window of the bar. Full control. No objective text: only the tape, now reading $1,912.00, and the door hanging open onto the street.

FIRST FIVE MINUTES (teaching through props, never pop-ups, nothing gated): shelves to climb, bottles lined up to be swatted, a gas fireplace and a candle (fire), a sink (water), a fuse box (electricity). Outside, a street tree whose trunk prompts [Sharpen claws]: the first contact with invulnerable nature is a gift, not a refusal. A dog that brings back whatever you throw. The bar sits 250 m from the west edge of the world on purpose.
Skipping the intro starts you on the bar counter with the treat already eaten.
concept_systems.core_loop:
30-SECOND LOOP (the toy): READ a setup (what is it made of, what is under it, what is it connected to) -> POKE it with one small cat verb -> WATCH the materials react and the chain run -> GRAB whatever the chain produced (a burning beam, a live cable, forty loose bricks, a tanker of milk) and use it as the next tool.

10-MINUTE LOOP (the heist of physics): CASE a block with Model Vision (stress colours, pipes, gas, building frequencies) -> RIG it (yarn lines, hairball fuses, scratch cuts, opened valves, a trench to steer the flood) -> TRIGGER it with a single swat -> RIDE it (cling to the falling tower, slow it, freeze it, rewind it and change one thing) -> READ THE TAPE: the claim form lists the causal chain ("Proximate cause: flowerpot") and pays Treats for every reaction you had never caused before.

2-HOUR LOOP (the district): find the district's Seam (a stolen tool) -> stage its biggest possible chain (its PML, "probable maximum loss") -> push it to Written Off (80% loss) -> nature reclaims it, animals move in, catnip grows -> the Model ships a patch that changes the rules for the districts still standing.

THE KEY TENSION: your paws start weak (tier 0 breaks only glass, wood, plaster and thin sheet). You cannot punch a tower down for hours. So from the first minute the efficient way to destroy big things is to make the world destroy itself: gravity, fire, water, gas, electricity, undermining. Chains multiply the recorded loss by up to x4 for indirectness; brute force never does. The game pays for cleverness and spectacle, never for grinding.

HANDS: the cat's body is on fixed buttons (swat/pounce, grab, jump/climb, meow, sprint); one "toy" slot is chosen from a radial wheel; the time family has its own three buttons; one key toggles Model Vision. The HUD is three things: the tape, nine Life pips, the toy icon.
concept_systems.world_design:
PORT INDEMNITY: a river city on a square slab of 1,280 x 1,280 m (80 x 80 chunks of 16 m), about 1.1 km of built-up area across. Heights: sea level 0 m, downtown +6 m, suburbs rising to +35 m, reservoir surface +48 m, hilltops +70 m; tallest building 140 m; 64 m of diggable ground under the streets. Edge to edge takes about 105 s at a cat's sprint (12 m/s) and 58 s with Zoomies (22 m/s). The river runs north to south from the dam to the harbour, so water, and floods, cross the whole map by gravity.
Content targets for the full game: about 280 structures (14 towers, 46 mid-rises, 84 rowhouses and shops, 72 houses, 34 industrial, 30 specials), 220 vehicles, 3 trains, 6 vessels, 900 trees, a ledger population of 1,200 humans and about 300 animals at the start. Every building is hollow with real floors; all ground floors and all hero buildings are dressed with props; nothing is a solid fake. Total insured value: about $20 billion.

Nine districts, each built around one destruction fantasy and one dominant system:

1. OLD QUAY (old town, west bank, 300 x 350 m). Brick, timber floors, slate, cobbles, gas lamps. Landmarks: The Ninth Life bar (start), the 38 m Clock Tower (Rewind Seam), the iron-and-glass Market Hall, a grand piano hanging from a removal hoist. Fantasy: DOMINOES AND FIRE. Masonry unzips brick by brick, fire runs through timber floors, the gas main under the high street launches manhole covers. PML: "The Great Fire of Old Quay", $0.9B.
2. PREMIUM HEIGHTS (downtown, east bank, 350 x 400 m). Steel-and-glass towers, concrete mid-rises, plazas, district steam, the subway. Landmarks: Solid Ground Tower (140 m, 34 floors, glass atrium, server floor = Red Dot Seam, a blimp moored to the roof), the twin Surety towers (90 m, standing exactly one tower-length apart), a glass skybridge. Fantasy: SKYSCRAPER PHYSICS. Heat-softened steel, curtain-wall glass cascades, lift shafts as chimneys, a tower felled into a tower. PML: "Tower Dominoes", $7B.
3. DEDUCTIBLE DOCKS (harbour and industry, south-west, 450 x 300 m). Sheet-metal sheds, container stacks five high, four 60 m gantry cranes, a 12-tank farm (fuel, water, acid, milk), a chemical works, a grain silo (dust explosions), a fireworks warehouse, a cargo ship. Fantasy: CHAIN REACTIONS AND FLUIDS. Tank bursts, burning fuel floating on the harbour, crane dominoes, container avalanches, sinking a ship at its berth. PML: "Tank Farm Cascade", $3B.
4. FAIRVIEW LAWNS (suburbs, east slope, 400 x 450 m). 72 timber houses with full interiors, pools, propane grills, trampolines, robot vacuums, indestructible hedges, a school, a strip mall, a 25 m water tower at the top of the hill. Fantasy: DOMESTIC SLAPSTICK AT CAT SCALE. 2,000 small props on tables and shelves, kitchen gas, a sinkhole swallowing a cul-de-sac, the water tower bowled down the main street. PML: "Sinkhole Street", $0.6B.
5. EXCESS DAM AND THE RESERVOIR (north). A concrete dam 180 m wide and 40 m high, a hydro station, a control room. Fantasy: THE FLOOD. A crack becomes a jet, the jet erodes a breach, and the wave runs 900 m of gorge to the sea in about 70 seconds, drowning the substation on the way. PML: "The Excess", $4B across four districts.
6. POLICY PIER (fairground, arena and mall, south-east, 250 x 200 m plus a 160 m timber pier). A 45 m Ferris wheel, a roller coaster, a bouncy castle, arcades, a photo booth (Freeze Frame Seam), an arena with a cable-net roof, a mall with a glass atrium. Fantasy: TOYS AT GIANT SCALE. The wheel rolls off its stand, coaster cars leave the track, the cable roof unzips. PML: "The Big Wheel", $0.8B.
7. THE LOOP (transit and power, ringing the centre). A 2.4 km elevated railway on 40 piers, 4 subway stations and 1.1 km of tunnel, the central substation ("the Hum") with 22 pylons, the 160 m cable-stayed Tollgate Bridge and a stone arch bridge. Fantasy: MOMENTUM AND NETWORKS. Derailments, pier-chopping, cutting bridge stays one at a time, rolling blackouts, a flooded or gas-filled subway. PML: "Lights Out", $2B.
8. THE GROUNDWORKS (quarry and construction, north-east, 300 x 250 m). A 35 m-deep quarry that shows the strata like a textbook, a bare 20-floor steel skeleton (the practice tower), a tower crane with a wrecking ball, a demolition-charge store, a cement works, and a patch of NO DATA exposed in the quarry floor (the Box Seam). Fantasy: THE ENGINEER'S PLAYGROUND, where the collapse rules are learned on a building with no skin. PML: "Skeleton Fall", $0.5B.
9. THE COMMONS AND CITY ZOO (central river island, 250 x 200 m). The 28 m Old Oak, a pond, a hedge maze, a glasshouse, and a small zoo of 12 enclosures (species depend on which free animal models exist; the dream cast is two elephants, two giraffes, capybaras, flamingos, penguins, a tortoise). Fantasy: LIBERATION. Every cage is man-made; nothing inside one can be hurt. No PML; instead "Open Day": free every enclosure.

WORLD TOYS, scattered everywhere (one obvious use, three non-obvious ones each): hydrants, propane tanks, transformers, vending machines, billboards, shopping trolleys, the insurer's blimp, a 6 m steel "ball of wool" sculpture parked on a slope, tanker trucks (fuel, water, acid, milk), two workmen carrying a sheet of glass across a road, the wrecking-ball crane.

The four edges differ: the sea to the south (it pours off the slab), hills and reservoir cut clean to the north, placeholder suburbs to the east, a looping highway to the west.
concept_systems.ground_layers:
The ground is a 64 m stack of strata (depths below street level in Premium Heights). The vertical scale is deliberately telescoped: real magma is kilometres down, but the Model only stores 64 m, and the deeper you go the more data-starved the world looks: coarser detail, flatter colour, rock faces stencilled INTERPOLATED.

0-0.4 m SURFACE PLATES. Asphalt on concrete, cobbles in Old Quay, paving slabs. Rigid fracture plates, not voxels: they crack, tilt and bridge holes. Do: break them open, or undermine them so they span a void until a bus drives over.
0.4-2 m ROAD BASE AND FILL. Loose gravel and sand: digs fast, slumps to a 35 degree slope, washes away in running water. Find: old tram rails, a time capsule (Treats). Do: wash it out with a broken main and you have made a real sinkhole.
1-6 m UTILITY ZONE. Colour-coded networks, visible in Model Vision, that you can bite into: water mains (blue), gas mains (yellow), power ducts (red), data fibre (purple: cut it and the block above drops to low-resolution textures while phones and cash machines glitch), district steam (silver), brick sewers 1.8 m across that a cat can run through, basements, footings and pile caps. Find: rats that guide you through the sewers. Do: most chains start here, and this is where buildings are undermined.
2-9 m SOIL, WITH A CLAY BAND AT 7.5-9 m. Soil + water = mud (weak and sticky; footings sink). Clay is watertight: floods pond on top of it; hole the clay and the flood drains away below. Clay + heat = hard ceramic, so you can fire your own lava-proof channel. Find: roots (protected), buried oddments.
6-14 m SUBWAY (under Premium Heights and Old Quay). Tunnels, four stations, running trains. Do: drop a street into it, flood it (it becomes the city's drain), or fill it with gas and light one end.
9-16 m AQUIFER. Saturated sand and gravel; water table at 9 m. Any pit deeper than 9 m fills to that level; basements and the subway flood if you connect them. Lava meeting the aquifer makes a steam blast that geysers out of your shaft.
16-22 m WEATHERED LIMESTONE. Soft rock, fossils, and abandoned mine galleries under the Groundworks and the upper suburbs, held up by old timber props (burn or cut the props and the street above subsides). Acid dissolves limestone fast: the Hork carves caves.
22-38 m BEDROCK (limestone grading into granite). Needs tier 3 claws, or tricks: heat rock and then douse it and it cracks one tier softer (the old miners' fire-setting), or borrow quarry charges. Find: a cave system with a lake and bats, crystal geodes (Treat caches), and a natural gas pocket at 30 m under the Docks (drill into it and gas climbs your shaft).
38-48 m BASALT HOT ZONE. Over 300 C: water flashes to steam, hairballs ignite, steel carried down here softens. Glowing cracks, hexagonal columns. Tier 4 claws.
48-58 m MAGMA CHAMBER (a lens about 500 m across under the city centre; solid basalt elsewhere). Pressurised. Breach it and lava climbs your shaft at 1 m/s: a narrow shaft gives a fountain at the surface (a volcano wherever you chose to dig), a wide pit gives a lava lake. Lava cannot hurt Rophe: touching it is a "hot beans" launch 30 m straight up, yowling, paws smoking (the prototype's magma bounce, kept as a traversal toy).
58-62 m NO DATA. Under the magma the Model has nothing. A cold, matte, shadowless crust drawn in flat diagonal map hatching that ignores perspective, stencilled NO DATA. Lava resting on it does not even glow at the contact. It is the softest material in the game: it shreds like cardboard.

BELOW THE LAST LAYER: THE UNDERWRITING. Tear through NO DATA and you fall out of the bottom of the world into the same void that surrounds it: the place under the world where it is written. Looking up you see the underside of the slab: foundations as stubs, every pipe and cable as a glowing coloured line, and under each building a hanging column of ledger rows (its value, its loss so far; destroyed buildings are stamped TOTAL LOSS). Far below lies the Table, an endless plane of ruled cells with numbers ticking. You fall, and are re-dropped from the sky like any other exit from the model.
Anything poured through a hole in NO DATA is deleted. Connect that hole to the harbour and the sea drains out through the bottom of the world.

Where the strata can be read without digging: the quarry wall in the Groundworks, and the cut face at every edge of the world.
concept_systems.edge_of_world:
The reveal is staged in rings, so the player senses that something is wrong long before they can name it. No green glyph rain and no green wireframe: this simulation is an insurer's hazard model, so what shows through is CARTOGRAPHY AND PAPERWORK.

1. THE FRINGE (150 m from the edge). Nothing glitches yet; things are merely cheap. Pedestrians turn around at an invisible line. The same three cars keep coming back with the same plates. Facade textures visibly tile. The distant skyline does not shift when you climb: it is a flat card. Reverb tails get shorter. Birdsong does not change at all.
2. THE MARGIN (60 m). The Model stops pretending. Contour lines appear on the ground at every metre of height, each line a string of tiny ledger text crawling at walking pace. Looking at any object unfolds its asset tag (material code, insured value, policy number). Shadows fall in steps. The last row of buildings is untextured white massing stencilled EXPOSURE PLACEHOLDER - VALUE ASSUMED. The humans here are padding records, all named PLACEHOLDER, J., standing nose to a wall. The trees and animals out here are the only things still rendered in full, loving detail.
3. THE GUTTER (15 m). The ground becomes the printed map it was made from: flat false colour, and lying on it at full size, the map furniture: a 12 m scale bar, a north arrow, and a legend block whose colour swatches are the game's 16 materials (a diegetic key to the whole reaction system). They are physics objects. You can knock the north arrow off the world. Snagging a loose contour line here gives you the Yarn; stealing the scale bar gives you Chonk.
4. THE EDGE. The slab ends in a clean vertical cut. The cut face is a 64 m cross-section of everything under the city, lit like a core sample and stencilled layer by layer: ASPHALT 0.4 / FILL / CLAY / AQUIFER / LIMESTONE / BASALT / MAGMA (EST.) / NO DATA. Basements, sewers and mine galleries are sliced open like an ant farm; a storm drain empties into space. To the south the sea pours off the edge in a waterfall that dissolves into hatching. Stepping off feels and sounds like pushing through a sheet of tracing paper.
5. THE FALL. Gravity continues. Rophe tumbles once and rights herself, feet down, tail steering. You pass the cross-section, then the underside of the slab with its hanging ledger columns.
6. THE VOID (the Underwriting): 7 seconds, or 2 if you hold the skip button. Indigo space; drifting contour strings you can bat for small rewards; enormous dice tumbling slowly in the distance (the random engine); hold music playing somewhere, slowed and waterlogged. Your statistics hang in the dark as giant figures: total loss, biggest chain, current return period. The void is the game's stats screen. A stamp slams across the view: EVENT OUT OF DOMAIN - RESAMPLING EPICENTRE, and map coordinates spin.
7. THE RE-DROP. A hatch-patterned hole opens in the sky and you fall out of it 250 m above a uniformly random point of the map (at least 100 m from any edge; never the same district twice running). You get 4 seconds of air-steering, about 60 m of freedom: enough to aim for the juiciest roof in sight, not enough to choose your district. Rophe always lands on four feet. Holding Pounce turns the landing into a strike: glass breaks within 15 m, a 1.5 m crater in asphalt, car alarms, and the tape prints EVENT RELOCATED. One landing in five is deliberately special: through a skylight into a living room, into a swimming pool, onto the roof of a moving train.

Because there is no death and the landing is fun, the edge works as slot-machine fast travel: jump off and see where the dice put you. Digging through the bottom of the world leads to the same void and the same re-drop. So does loading a saved game (onto your saved position instead of a random one), which means the fall also hides loading.
concept_systems.destruction_model:
PRINCIPLE: nothing has hit points and nothing has a scripted destruction. Things have a material, a place in a structure, and neighbours. Damage is energy; collapse is lost support; everything else is the reaction table.

1. HOW THINGS ARE BUILT. A building is a graph of structural ELEMENTS (footing, column, bearing wall, beam, floor slab, panel, glazing, stair, roof) of about 3 m, joined to their neighbours: about 150 elements for a house, about 3,000 for the tallest tower. Each element is pre-cut into 6-40 shards. Elements sleep as merged static geometry until something happens within 20 m; then they wake individually; only pieces that really come loose become physics bodies. Vehicles and props are the same idea at smaller scale (a car is 16 parts: panels, glass, wheels, fuel tank, battery).

2. HOW THINGS BREAK. Impact energy (half mass times speed squared) is spent against the element's toughness. Partial damage removes the shards nearest the hit, so a thrown brick makes a brick-sized hole, and holes grow. Glass and ceramic shatter; wood splinters along the grain and bends first; masonry comes apart along its mortar into single bricks; reinforced concrete crumbles but hangs on its rebar until the rebar is cut or melted; steel never shatters: it bends, buckles and tears at the joints.

3. MATERIAL TABLE (the reaction matrix; a data file the director can edit)
Material | Claw tier | Breaks as | Heat and fire | Water | Electricity | Acid | Note
Glass | 0 | radial shards, glitter rubble | cracks at 300 C; hot glass + water shatters at once; slumps at 900 C | holds fluids | insulates | immune (the acid jar) | scored glass breaks at 25% energy
Ceramic, porcelain | 0 | sharp shards | fireproof; a bathtub holds lava for 60 s | holds fluids | insulates | immune | the lava bucket
Paper, fabric, cardboard | 0 | tears | flash-burns in 5 s, carries fire fast | soaked = will not burn | insulates | gone in 2 s | claim forms are this
Plaster, drywall | 0 | powdery chunks, much dust | chars, does not sustain | mush, -70% strength | insulates | fast | dust can explode indoors
Plastic, rubber | 0 | snaps | melts at 200 C, thick black smoke | floats | insulates (use it) | immune | smoke blinds and panics
Wood | 0-1 | long splinters | ignites at 300 C, burns 40-90 s to weak charcoal, throws embers | wet wood will not light for 60 s; floats | conducts only when wet | slow |
Sheet metal, aluminium | 1 | dents, tears | aluminium melts at 660 C | sealed hulls float | conducts | very fast (5 s) | cars, containers, ducts
Asphalt | 1 | slabs and crumbs | sticky at 150 C, burns oily at 400 C | - | insulates | slow | lava makes a tar pool
Brick masonry | 1 | single bricks along mortar | fireproof; mortar weak above 600 C | mortar -20% when soaked | insulates | mortar first: the wall unzips | the best throwing ammo
Concrete | 2 | angular chunks, dust | spalls above 500 C | - | insulates | 12 s per 0.5 m |
Stone: limestone / granite | 2 / 3 | blocks | heat then water cracks it one tier softer | - | insulates | limestone fast, granite immune |
Reinforced concrete | 3 | chunks dangling on rebar | rebar softens at 600 C, slab sags | - | rebar conducts (hidden paths through buildings) | concrete medium, rebar fast |
Structural steel | 4 | bends, buckles, tears at joints | 50% strength at 550 C, 10% at 900 C; never burns | - | conducts | 30 s per beam | fire brings down what paws cannot
Loose ground: soil, sand, gravel, rubble | 0 | flows, slumps at 35 degrees | sand + lava or Red Dot = glass | soil becomes mud; flow erodes it | conducts when wet | soil neutralises acid | smothers fire
Clay | 1 | plastic lumps | fires to ceramic | watertight | - | slow |
Electronics | 0 | sparks and smoke | - | shorts, small fire | overload pops it | fast | lamps, signals, servers, transformers
FLUIDS: water; fuel (floats on water and burns on top of it); acid; lava (cools to basalt in 40 s, or at once in water with a steam burst); milk (water that attracts cats). GASES: fuel gas (fills rooms from the ceiling down; the blast scales with how enclosed it is); steam (pressure: boilers and sealed pipes burst); smoke (rises, blinds, panics); dust (explosive in closed rooms).

4. STRUCTURAL COLLAPSE: five rules, all visible as colours in Model Vision
- ANCHOR: every element needs an unbroken chain of joints to a footing, and every footing needs ground. Remove half the voxels under a footing, or turn them to mud or lava, and it lets go.
- SPAN: support fades sideways. An unsupported run survives 1 bay in masonry, 2 in timber, 3 in reinforced concrete, 5 in steel; one more and it drops.
- LOAD: every column and bearing wall has a capacity (a brick wall carries 4 storeys, a concrete column 30, a steel column 45), reduced by heat, soaking, acid loss and damage. Overload means cracking, a groan and a dust jet, then failure 0.4-2.5 s later, which hands the load to the neighbours: progressive collapse, staggered so you can watch it travel.
- FALL TOGETHER: whatever is cut off from every anchor falls as one rigid cluster (the top ten floors come down as a block) and breaks up only on impact. A falling cluster crushes each floor beneath it in 0.15-0.3 s if its energy beats the slab: the pancake.
- CUT SIDE IS FALL SIDE: remove 60% of the ground-floor supports on one side and the building hinges on the rest and topples toward the cut, like felling a tree. Predictable enough to aim, which is what makes tower-into-tower possible.

5. DEBRIS LIFECYCLE: NOTHING VANISHES, IT CHANGES REPRESENTATION
- LIVE: tumbling physics bodies (target 1,200 awake at once).
- RESTING: asleep where they stopped; still grabbable, kickable, burnable (target 6,000).
- RUBBLE: after 90 s at rest, and only off-screen, behind dust or more than 25 m away, small shards are baked into the ground as RUBBLE VOXELS in the right colour mix (red brick scree, grey concrete, glittering glass) at 1.3 times their volume. A fallen tower leaves a hill of about a fifth of its original volume with its largest beams and slabs sticking out. Rubble is a ground layer: dig it, kick it, flood it, tunnel in it, vacuum it into the Box; the Scruff pulls throwable chunks back out of it.
- WRECKS: anything longer than 2 m (beams, slabs, car bodies, crane booms) stays for good as a recognisable static wreck that wakes again when touched, pulled or blasted.
- OVERGROWN: about 10 minutes later, or at once when a district is Written Off, moss, grass, flowers and vines dress the rubble and animals move in.
The 90 s bake delay is longer than the longest rewind (30 s), so anything you can rewind is still made of real pieces.

6. CHAIN REACTIONS. Districts are wired together by networks under the streets: gas, water, sewers, power, data, steam, rail, traffic. A typical cross-map chain: dam breach -> flood wave -> substation shorts -> blackout -> signals die -> tanker crash -> burning fuel floats downstream on the flood -> the docks. Every damage event remembers what caused it, so the game can count chain depth, print the chain on the claim tape, and multiply the loss by 1 + 0.25 per link (maximum x4).

7. THE WORLD KEEPS BURNING WITHOUT YOU. The simulation has three levels of detail: cell-accurate within 96 m, element-level out to 300 m, building-level beyond (a fire lit in Old Quay really does take the district while you are at the docks). When load spikes, a chaos governor slows world time to as little as 0.4x, which reads as deliberate cinematic slow motion, and spawns the smallest fragments as particles. It never deletes anything in view.

tools_and_powers.name: Swat and Pounce (innate)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Swat: a 1.2 m paw strike that puts a precise impulse exactly where it lands (150 newton-seconds at the start: launches a bottle, tips a television; x4 per rank tier, ending at van-flipping). Pounce: hold 0.6 s, leap up to 8 m high and 14 m far; the landing does damage equal to your kinetic energy, so height is ammunition: a dive from a 60 m roof at tier 3 goes through a reinforced floor and leaves a 2 m crater.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: It is the thesis verb, knock it off the table, and it makes climbing matter: the higher you get, the harder you land.

tools_and_powers.name: Claws: Climb, Cling, Shred (innate)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Climb any man-made surface and any tree trunk at 4 m/s with no stamina bar. Grip depends on material: brick, wood, concrete and steel lattice are full grip; glass and polished panels are zero grip, so you slide down at 3 m/s with a screech, leaving three score lines (scored glass breaks at a quarter of the usual energy). Cling to anything moving or falling and hop between falling chunks. Hold Shred while clinging to peel cladding, signage and cable off a facade in long strips.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Requirement 5 as a toy: you can ride a toppling tower all the way down, and sliding down a glass tower quietly pre-weakens it for later.

tools_and_powers.name: Scratch: Three-Line Cut (rank 1-in-10)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: A ranged claw slash that draws three parallel cut planes 0.3 m apart (reach 6 m growing to 25 m, depth 0.5 m growing to 3 m) and cleanly severs any element up to your hardness tier along the direction you swiped. No fracture, no debris: a cut. A diagonal cut through a column makes the top slide off toward the low side. Five charges; resharpen on any tree trunk.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Precision, the opposite of Swat. This is the tool for aiming a collapse: cut side is fall side.

tools_and_powers.name: Scruff: Grab, Carry, Throw (innate)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Grab any loose piece, prop, human or vehicle inside your mass tier (25 kg, 250 kg, 2.5 t, 25 t) and carry it 1.5 m ahead of your mouth. Charge to throw at up to 45 m/s. Objects keep their state in flight: burning, soaked, live, acid-coated. Hold the Hoard key to add up to 8 more pieces to an orbiting ring, then fire them one by one or as a volley. Also pulls throwable chunks back out of rubble piles.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Every chain reaction leaves you a new weapon; the wreckage of the world is your ammunition belt.

tools_and_powers.name: Litterbox: Dig and Kick (innate)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Dig the ground at 0.5 to 6 cubic metres per second depending on stratum and tier. The spoil is real: it sprays out behind you in a 30 degree fan and lands as loose material. Aim the spray as a weapon (gravel is shrapnel), as a fire blanket (soil smothers flames), or to bury something, which is very cat. Trenches steer water, fuel, acid and lava; a buried gas leak builds pressure and blows out later.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Digging is not a menu action but a mess you make, and trenching turns every fluid in the game into something you can route.

tools_and_powers.name: Meow and Yowl (innate)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Tap for a Mew: a 12 m startle that herds humans and animals, trips car alarms and rattles loose props. Hold for a Yowl: a 30 degree, 35 m pressure cone that shatters glass and pushes smoke, gas clouds, flames, embers and light debris along at 15 m/s. A short burst blows out small fires; a sustained yowl feeds them air and doubles their intensity.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: It is the steering wheel for the invisible systems: you blow a fire across a street and walk a gas cloud to a spark.

tools_and_powers.name: Purrquake (rank 1-in-50)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Hold to purr into the ground: a vibration 20 to 80 m across whose pitch you set between 0.25 and 8 Hz. Every building has a natural frequency of about 10 divided by its number of floors (a house 5 Hz, a 10-storey block 1 Hz, the tallest tower 0.3 Hz). Hold within 15 percent of it and the sway builds over 6 seconds: joints fatigue, masonry cracks first, glass pops. In wet sand or soil the ground liquefies: buildings sink and tilt up to 15 degrees and buried tanks float up.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Real earthquake engineering reduced to one dial: you tune the cat to the building, and you can hear when you have found the note.

tools_and_powers.name: Hairball (innate)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Cough a sticky wad (9 in stock, 1 back every 8 s) that stays where it lands. It is a wick: a trail of hairballs burns at 1 m/s. It is a sponge: it takes on the first fluid it touches, becoming a firebomb (fuel), a 40-litre water balloon (water) or a corrosive plug that eats a half-metre hole in 8 s (acid). Wet, it conducts. Hold the button to lay a continuous strand up to 60 m long.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: One humble object becomes fuse, timer, bomb, extinguisher and wire depending on what you dip it in: the systems multiply the toolbox for free.

tools_and_powers.name: The Hork (rank 1-in-50)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: After the unmistakable three-heave wind-up, a 12 m arc of acid at 6 litres per second for 5 seconds (20 s to refill). Acid is a real fluid: it pools, runs downhill, drips through the hole it makes, dilutes in water and is neutralised by soil. It eats sheet metal in 5 s, limestone in 6, mortar in 8, concrete in 12, a steel beam in 30; glass, ceramic and plastic are immune, so a fish bowl can carry it.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: A slow vertical drill that keeps working after you leave, with a wind-up every cat owner will recognise. It replaces the prototype's acid beam with something that behaves like a liquid.

tools_and_powers.name: Static (rank 1-in-10)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Fur charge from 0 to 100, built by sprinting (carpet, nylon and rubber charge three times faster) and lost by getting wet or touching earthed metal. Discharge at 25: a 2 m spark that lights gas, fuel and hairballs and trips electronics. At 60: a 10 m arc that chains through up to six conductors. At 100: a 30 m bolt and a 25 m pulse that pops every lamp, stalls every engine and trips transformers into a blackout. Storms charge you constantly.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Electricity you earn by running laps on a hotel carpet; a blackout rolling across the night skyline is the best reward shot in the game. There is no fireball: fire is a state you cause, not a projectile.

tools_and_powers.name: Zoomies and the Twister (sprint innate; Twister at rank 1-in-100)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Zoomies: a 22 m/s sprint with wall-running and doubled jump height. Run three full circles within 6 seconds and the circle becomes a Twister as wide as your lap (4 to 20 m radius) for 20 seconds, following you on a 40 m leash. It lifts loose bodies up to your grab tier and loose material from the ground and the Field: rubble makes a shredder, fire makes a fire whirl throwing embers 60 m, floodwater makes a spout that rains wherever you lead it.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: The 3 a.m. cat sprint turned into weather, and the tool that turns a pile of old wreckage back into a weapon.

tools_and_powers.name: Yarn (Seam: a loose contour line at the Edge)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Fire one end at A and the other at B (40 m range), then choose: Winch (contracts at 2 m/s with 5 kN, 50 kN, 500 kN or 5 MN by upgrade), Slack (a rope) or Swing (hold to grapple and swing yourself). Up to nine lines at once. Either the line or whatever it is tied to gives way first. Yarn burns as a 2 m/s fuse and conducts when wet. A line tied to a tree can never be pulled loose.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Climbing aid, demolition rig, tripwire, fuse and power cable in one; nine lines winched together is a controlled implosion.

tools_and_powers.name: The Box (Seam: the NO DATA patch in the quarry floor)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: A cardboard box that opens onto NO DATA. Inhale vacuums up fluids, gases, loose ground, rubble, props and humans (they come out dizzy) to a capacity of 2, 20 or 200 cubic metres; contents keep their temperature and state. Pour them out at 0.5 to 20 cubic metres per second or dump everything at once. Set the Box down as a proximity mine, throw it so it bursts on impact, or hide in it: Loss Prevention never checks an empty box.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: The bucket tool every material sandbox needs: carry a lava lake to the top of a tower, a roomful of gas to a bonfire, the reservoir to the suburbs.

tools_and_powers.name: The Red Dot (Seam: the server floor of Solid Ground Tower)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: The analyst's cursor. Steer a red dot over any surface in line of sight up to 300 m; a silent beam from the sky heats that spot by 150 C per second: wood lights in 2 s, steel reaches its softening point in 4 s and is cut through in 8, glass slumps in 6, sand fuses to glass, clay fires to ceramic, water flashes to steam. Battery 10 s, recharging 1 s every 3 s. Other cats chase it, so it also leads your Colony. Double-tap and Rophe pounces to the dot from up to 60 m away.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Surgical heat from a rooftop, and the purest cat joke available: the most dangerous weapon in the game is a laser pointer.

tools_and_powers.name: Chonk and Smol (Seam: the scale bar lying at the Edge)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: You stole the map's scale. Grow to x4, x12 or x40 (12 m at the shoulder); time is banked from destruction at 1 s per $1M of fresh loss, 60 s maximum. Mass rises with the cube, so swats go through walls. 'If I Fits, I Sits': choose a roof, a bus or a bridge deck and sit; the load ramps to three times your weight over 5 s as the loaf settles, until the structure's load rule gives up. Or shrink to x0.25 and run inside pipes, ducts and wall cavities to cut wires and open valves from within.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: The giant-monster fantasy and the mouse-hole fantasy from one dial, both obeying the same structural rules as everything else.

tools_and_powers.name: Echoes: Nine Lives (Seam: first visit to the Underwriting)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Record up to 10 seconds of your own actions, then spawn an Echo: a translucent past self that repeats them on a loop, exactly in time. Up to eight Echoes, so nine cats. Echoes pass through debris, but their swats, cuts, throws, yowls and purrs are real. Hiss to dismiss them all.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: One cat cannot cut eight columns in the same instant; nine can. It turns the player into a demolition crew, or a purring choir on one note.

tools_and_powers.name: Rewind (Seam: the mechanism of the Old Quay Clock Tower, about 20 minutes in)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Hold to run the entire world backwards at 1x to 3x through the last 10 seconds (20 and 30 with upgrades): shards knit, towers stand up, floods recede, folded humans unfold. Costs Nine Lives pips; a full meter equals one full window. Release and time continues from that instant with all motion restored. Exact rules are in the time_rewind section.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Undo for a sandbox: try the same collapse five ways, or just watch a skyscraper un-fall because it is beautiful.

tools_and_powers.name: Freeze Frame (Seam: the photo booth on Policy Pier)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Stop world time for up to 6 s (10 upgraded) while Rophe moves freely. Frozen debris, water, flames and blast waves become solid and harmless: stand on them, climb them, rearrange whatever you can carry. Every hit you land on a frozen object is banked and released together when time restarts.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: It turns any explosion into a climbing frame and any object into a spring you can wind up: nine swats on a frozen bus, then let go.

tools_and_powers.name: Cat Reflexes: slow motion (innate)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: World at 0.2x speed, Rophe at 0.6x, for up to 8 s on its own meter, which refills from chain reactions. Also triggers by itself for 1.5 s when a chain crosses a new size threshold (can be switched off).
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Precision throws through a collapsing floor, and the honest pleasure of watching glass break slowly.

tools_and_powers.name: Director's Cut: replay and photo mode (from the start)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Pause and scrub back through the last 30 s (120 s of large pieces with the Black Box upgrade) with a free camera, speed control from 0.05x to 4x, depth of field, filters and HUD off. It is view-only: leaving it returns you to the present untouched. Saves stills, and every finished chain auto-generates a shareable claim-form image listing its causal chain.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Destruction games are sold by clips. This makes every player a trailer editor.

concept_systems.time_rewind:
ONE SYSTEM, FOUR VERBS. The game continuously records a Timeline: 30 samples per second of every awake body, plus an event log (fractures, broken joints, voxel edits together with what was there before, valve and switch states, human states) and a sparse snapshot of the Field every 0.5 s. Rewind, Freeze Frame, slow motion and Replay are four ways of reading that one recording. It is a recording, not a re-simulation, so it does not depend on the physics engine being deterministic.

REWIND, exactly:
- Hold the key: the whole world runs backwards at 1x (3x with the boost button). Shards fly home and knit, towers stand up, lava drains back down its shaft, floodwater recedes, folded humans unfold, the adding-machine tape reels back in and un-prints. Sound plays reversed and pitched down.
- Window: the last 10 s at first; 20 s and 30 s with upgrades.
- Cost: the Nine Lives meter, 9 pips. A full meter always equals one full window; partial rewinds spend in proportion. Refill: 1 pip per 12 s, plus 1 pip for every chain of five links or more. 1.5 s lock-out after release.
- Release: time runs forward again from that instant with every velocity restored. Doing nothing replays almost the same collapse (small pieces land differently). Changing ONE thing, a hairball here, a cut there, is the point: rewind is the sandbox's undo and its director's chair.
- Rophe rewinds with the world by default. Upgrade "Stay Put": hold the modifier and the world rewinds around a cat who stays where she is (stand in the crater, rewind, and you are inside the lobby before it happened). If something un-breaks where you are standing, it gently pushes you out.
- What does NOT rewind: tools, upgrades, Treats, Claims Book discoveries and your best recorded event. Rewinding can never cost the player progress, so it is always a free choice. The loss total does rewind, so loops cannot be farmed.
- Hard limits: only the window; never across loading a save. Individually recorded pieces are capped at 1,200; beyond that, small shards are not replayed from the recording but flown along smooth arcs back to their known slots in the parent element, which is cheap and looks right because all fracture is pre-cut. Fire, gas and water are restored from the half-second snapshots and blended, so they reverse approximately, not exactly. Rubble already baked into the ground is older than any window and is never touched.

FREEZE FRAME: world time stops for up to 6 s (10 with upgrade); Rophe moves normally. Frozen debris, water, flame and blast fronts become solid and harmless: you can run up a frozen explosion. Every hit you land is banked and released at once on unfreeze (nine swats on a frozen bus is a x9 launch). Costs 1 pip per second. Releasing a rewind while holding Freeze hands you the past, frozen.
CAT REFLEXES (slow motion): world at 0.2x, Rophe at 0.6x, up to 8 s on its own meter refilled by chains; fires automatically for 1.5 s when a chain crosses a new threshold (optional).
DIRECTOR'S CUT (replay): view-only scrub through the Timeline with a free camera, speed control, depth of field and filters; leaving it returns you to the present unchanged. The "Black Box" upgrade keeps 120 s of large bodies only.

BUILD ORDER: rigid-body and fracture rewind first (it is the showpiece and the robust part), voxel edits second, Field rewind last.
concept_systems.npcs:
HUMANS (policyholders). About 1,200 on the ledger; 150-200 simulated near the player, the rest counted per district. Archetypes by district (office workers, dockers, builders, families, tourists, the bartender) plus four professions that feed the systems: firefighters (bring real water to real fires, which can short real electrics), repair crews (close valves, re-energise feeders), a news van and helicopter (they film you; billboard tickers print headlines generated from your causal chains: LOCAL CAT LINKED TO FERRIS WHEEL INCIDENT), and Loss Prevention (the Model's cat-catchers).
Five states: Routine (walk, work, queue, sit) -> Curious (phones out; some try to pet you) -> Alarmed (flee; panic spreads by sight and sound through a crowd) -> Respond (professionals only) -> Claimed. Their danger map is the Field itself: they avoid heat, smoke, water and live puddles, so you can herd a crowd with a Yowl-steered smoke cloud or strand an office on its own roof. They evacuate to the parks, which is logical (nothing there can fall on them) and funny (hundreds of people hiding behind indestructible hedges).
Loss Prevention carry nets, spray bottles, cucumbers and cat carriers. None of it can hurt you; all of it is slapstick and all of it is a toy. The spray bottle empties your Static and shoves you 3 m. A cucumber makes Rophe leap 6 m straight up whether you like it or not (a jump pad you learn to use). A net leads to a carrier and a van; do nothing for 20 s and you get a 30 s Vet Cone (narrower view, but your Meow carries twice as far through it). You can burst out of the van after 5 s, and then you have a van.

HARM: NON-GORY AND COMIC (recommended). Light hits knock humans over: they ragdoll for 2-4 s, get up dizzy and run. Past a threshold (crushed, burned, a long fall, a blast) a human is CLAIMED: they freeze for one frame in a ridiculous pose, fold flat with a paper snap into a claim form, and the form flutters down stamped PAID with their name and a one-line cause of loss ("struck by vending machine; cause: cat"). Whatever they were carrying drops as props. The forms are real paper: they blow about, clog drains and burn. No blood, no bodies, and it reads as simulation. In a rewind they unfold again. While a district still stands, claimed residents are re-issued as lower-detail PLACEHOLDER people; a Written Off district has none.
Alternatives considered: (a) ragdoll only, nobody is ever lost: safest, but it makes "humans can be harmed" untrue and the crowd weightless; I ship it as the optional GENTLE MODE toggle. (b) Realistic injury: wrong tone, wrong rating, bad for streaming and store visibility, and needs art nobody here can make. (c) Humans as obvious robots or mannequins: kills the slapstick. Paper wins.

ANIMALS (not in exposure). About 300 at the start, about 1,500 once the city has gone wild. Pigeons and gulls (they lift off in a wave from every blast, the best free impact effect in the game, then land on the wreckage); crows (leave them shiny shards and they bring you a Treat); dogs (chase you, and fetch whatever you throw, girders included); stray cats (the Colony: up to 8 followers who copy your swats at small scale; milk spills recruit them); rats (sewer guides); ducks and swans (ride the floodwater); koi (break a pond and each fish stays inside its own wobbling ball of water, commuting through the air to the next pond); bats; and the zoo animals once freed.
Three states: Routine, Startle (a two-second hop, then calm: the comic contrast with screaming humans) and Herd (a Meow moves a group away from you in a line). They are never hurt, never trapped and never afraid for long.
concept_systems.nature_rule:
IN-FICTION REASON. The Model only contains damage functions for insured things. Trees, plants and animals were never insured, so they are "not in exposure": the catastrophe cannot compute a loss for them, therefore nothing happens to them. The same line protects Rophe, which is why there is no death. The Claims Book puts it in one line: "No policy. No damage curve. Lucky them."

THE RULE, STATED SO THE PLAYER CAN PREDICT IT (six lines):
1. TRUNKS, BRANCHES AND HEDGES are solid and are the hardest things in the world. Debris piles against them; a falling facade is split in two by a tree; a blast is shadowed behind one.
2. LEAVES, FLOWERS, GRASS AND ALL ANIMALS let flying things through: debris, blast and thrown objects pass with a soft ripple, so nothing living is ever crushed or buried and your throw is never wasted on a pigeon.
3. NOTHING GREEN BURNS, conducts, corrodes or melts. Fire stops at a park or a hedge and can only cross as embers you carry, throw or blow. Lava parts around a trunk and leaves it on a cooled island. Floods just lift the ducks.
4. ROOTS HOLD THEIR EARTH: a cone of soil 1.5 m wide and 3 m deep under every tree cannot be dug. Excavate a park and each tree is left on its own floating plug of soil, roots dangling: the Model refuses to drop it.
5. SMALL PLANTS COME BACK: any bare soil or rubble open to the sky grows grass within a minute. Dig a pit in a lawn and it lines itself in green; a smashed flowerpot's plant re-roots where it lands.
6. ANIMALS MOVE THE WORLD, THE WORLD NEVER MOVES ANIMALS: a walking animal shoulders standing props, cars and humans aside; nothing pushes back.

HOW IT IS COMMUNICATED. In Model Vision everything man-made is false-colour with a tag; nature and animals stay in full natural colour with no tag: readable at a glance. The aim reticle becomes a small leaf on anything protected. The first three times a player attacks nature: a soft chime, a shimmer, and a small stamp NOT IN EXPOSURE; after that only the chime. And the first tree in the game teaches the rule as a gift (claw sharpening), not as a refusal.

THE RULE AS A FEATURE (the important part):
- SCRATCHING POSTS: tree trunks resharpen your Scratch charges. Nature is your workshop.
- IMMOVABLE ANCHORS: a Yarn line tied to a tree cannot be pulled loose. Tie a tower to the Old Oak and winch. Two trees and a tensioned line make a slingshot that fires a car 200 m.
- CLEAVERS AND BLAST WALLS: fell a building onto a tree line to cut it into slices; park a fuel tanker behind a hedge to save it for later.
- FIREBREAK TACTICS: because green stops fire, burning a city is a routing puzzle, and the Yowl, the Twister and thrown embers are how you solve it.
- THE STAMPEDE: herd freed zoo animals or a field of cows with Meow; being unstoppable, they walk through fences, market stalls, shopfronts and parked cars like a slow, placid wrecking crew.
- LIVING BRIDGES: animals crossing lava leave cooled stepping stones behind them. Follow the tortoise.
- REWILDING, the loop-closer: every ruin goes green, and overgrown rubble sprouts CATNIP. Rolling in it triggers Catnip Frenzy for 25 s: every tool one tier stronger, time at 0.6x, and the full psychedelic false-colour trip with contour lines pulsing to the music. Destroying the man-made world literally grows the fuel for destroying more of it, and the map shows progress as spreading green instead of spreading grey. Flooded ruins rewild twice as fast.

The end state of a finished save is not a wasteland: it is a wild valley full of animals with a cat asleep in it.
concept_systems.progression_and_goals:
NO MISSIONS, NO CHECKLISTS, NO TIMERS, NO FAIL STATE. Four pulls, all optional, all fed by play you would do anyway.

1. CURIOSITY: THE CLAIMS BOOK. About 110 entries, one per distinct reaction or event the systems can produce ("thermal shock", "fuel fire on floodwater", "felled a building onto a building", "a dog fetched a girder", "reached the aquifer"). Undiscovered entries are redacted claim forms with a silhouette. Each first-time discovery pays 1-3 Treats. This is the pixel-sandbox reward: finding out what reacts with what.
2. MAGNITUDE: RETURN PERIOD. Your rank is the rarity of your single biggest chain (the loss inside one causal chain, with the indirectness multiplier): Nuisance (1-in-2 years, start) -> Incident (1-in-10, $50k) -> Local Emergency (1-in-50, $1M) -> Named Event (1-in-100, $10M; the news starts calling you Event Rophe) -> Solvency Test (1-in-250, $50M) -> Market-Turning Event (1-in-1,000, $250M) -> Act of Cat (1-in-10,000, $1B) -> Unmodelled (after the ending). Ranks raise the claw hardness tier (0 at start, 1 at 1-in-10, 2 at 1-in-50, 3 at 1-in-250, 4 at 1-in-1,000) and the grab mass (25 kg, 250 kg, 2.5 t, 25 t). Because rank comes from one great event and not from accumulated damage, the way to progress is to stage something magnificent, never to grind.
3. PLACE: SEAMS, PMLs AND WRITE-OFFS. Seven Seams (spots where the Model shows through) each give a stolen tool. Each district has a PML, the biggest chain its layout allows, hinted at by a half-redacted memo; reaching 80% of it in a single event earns a gold stamp. A district at 80% total loss is Written Off: permanent, green, and no longer rebuilt or patched.
4. OPPOSITION: PATCH NOTES. At 10 / 25 / 40 / 55% citywide loss the Model ships a patch that changes the rules in the districts still standing, each one beaten through a different system: v9.1 sprinklers in commercial buildings (cut the water main first); v9.2 automatic gas shut-off valves (find and break the valve cabinets); v9.3 river flood gates and Loss Prevention drones (black out the gate motors); v9.4 seismic retrofit and backup generators (fire and acid still work). Difficulty rises by making you think, never by adding hit points.

Treats (about 150 in the game) buy upgrades: rewind window, Box volume, Yarn strength, Echo count, hairball stock. Opt-in DARES are printed on the back of claim forms ("Total a bus without touching it").

FIRST HOUR: 0-5 min the bar; 5-20 min Old Quay streets, first fire, rank 1-in-10; about 20 min the Clock Tower and Rewind; 30-60 min the first trip to the edge, the Yarn, the first fall and re-drop.

ENDING: YES, OPTIONAL, AT ABOUT 8-12 HOURS. Conditions: Solid Ground Tower is down, citywide loss is 60% or more, and you have been under the world. Final patch note: "v9.9.9: restoring from backup." The Model starts rewinding your ruins back into buildings; you drop into the Underwriting and shred three giant backup spools hanging under the slab while the city above un-collapses and re-collapses. Then: RESTORE FAILED - TOTAL LOSS. The camera pulls back until the city is a model on the Table. One prompt: [Swat]. Credits over the wild valley, then the desk-and-keyboard stinger.
AFTER THE ENDING: your world is restored to the moment before the finale and stays open for good. Unlocked: NEW EVENT (a fresh world with a new seed, the patches active from the start, your Claims Book kept), free REINSTATE of any district to pristine at any time, and THE LAB (a flat test range where anything can be spawned). A destruction sandbox must never run out of things to break.
concept_systems.save_system:
YES: persistent destruction is the whole promise, so saving is not optional. Three parts.

1. CONTINUOUS AUTOSAVE (invisible). One world file per slot, three slots. It saves every 90 s when no chain is running, and on every rank-up, tool unlock, district write-off and on quit. Quitting never loses anything.
2. NAPS (manual snapshots, diegetic). Curl up in any sunbeam, or inside the Box, by holding the Nap key for 2 s: the game stores a snapshot, named for you ("Before the dam - $1.2B") with a thumbnail. Nine snapshot slots per world: nine lives. Restoring one is "waking up earlier". This is what lets a player spend 20 minutes rigging a block, try it, and try it again differently. Broken roofs let in more sunbeams, so wrecked districts have more nap spots.
3. RESETS. Reinstate District (back to pristine, unlocks kept, free) and New Event (a new world).

WHAT IS STORED (compact, because a world is "pristine city + differences"): the state of every building element (intact / which shards are missing / gone), voxel edits per 16 m chunk (run-length encoded and compressed), permanent wrecks (up to 4,000 positions), standing water and cooled lava (as ground edits and per-region water levels), network states (valves, breaks, dead feeders), rewilding timers, human and animal counts per district, player state, the Claims Book, the random seed. Target 5-15 MB per world, hard cap 40 MB.
WHAT IS NOT STORED: the rewind Timeline, velocities of pieces in flight, individual NPC positions, live flames. On load, pieces in flight are settled by a hidden two-second fast-forward, and fires are resolved by the long-distance rule (burned out or scorched).
LOADING IS A RE-DROP: every load begins with the fall from the sky onto your saved position. It hides streaming and settling and needs no extra fiction.
SAFETY: write to a temporary file and then rename it; keep two rolling backups; put a version number in the header and write migration code from day one (a ten-hour destroyed world lost to an update would be unforgivable).
PLATFORMS: saves live in the engine's per-user folder. On Steam, Auto-Cloud can sync that folder without code; the itch.io build uses the same local files.
concept_systems.art_and_audio_direction:
LOOK: SCALE-MODEL REALISM. The city should look like the most beautiful architect's model ever built, seen from 30 cm off the ground: clean physically-based materials, slightly simplified forms, crisp edges, real shadows, and a hint of tilt-shift depth of field whenever the camera pulls back. It fits the fiction (this is a model, on a table), it flatters free mid-poly assets, and it gives the game a face no other destruction sandbox has.

HOW MIXED FREE ASSETS BECOME ONE WORLD (the pipeline matters more than the sources): every imported model is stripped of its original textures and re-skinned by material tag from one library of 16 tiling PBR materials with consistent texel density, plus per-material fracture interiors (aggregate inside concrete, rebar stubs, brick cores, wood grain) and procedural grime and edge wear. Sources: Kenney, Quaternius and KayKit modular kits (CC0) as the structural base; Poly Haven and ambientCG (CC0) for surfaces and skies; Sketchfab and itch.io for hero pieces, CC0 or CC-BY only, never NC or ND; every file is entered in a licence ledger that generates the credits screen.
THE CAT is the one asset that must be excellent: the best rigged free cat available, plus procedural layers the agent can code (tail spring, ear and head look-at, spine lean into turns, landing squash, paw placement on ledges, fur puffing up with Static). If the cat does not feel alive, nothing else matters.
LIGHT AND AIR: golden hour by default on a 40-minute day cycle; real-time global illumination and ambient occlusion; volumetric dust hanging in light shafts after every collapse; fires that actually light the street; at night, lit windows that go dark block by block in a blackout.
EVERY BREAK HAS FOUR LAYERS: the fracture itself, dust and particles, a persistent mark (crack, scorch, wet patch, stain) and the material's own sound. Heavy hits add 40-80 ms of hit-stop, a camera kick and rumble.
CAMERA: at cat height, pulling back and up by itself when a collapse starts so the whole event stays in frame.

THE MODEL'S OWN IDENTITY (original: nothing green, no glyph rain, no wireframe): CARTOGRAPHY AND PAPERWORK. A false-colour hazard palette (ink indigo, violet, hot magenta, amber, paper white); contour lines made of crawling ledger text; flat diagonal hatching for NO DATA; registration marks at the corners of the 16 m grid; rubber stamps; triplicate-form colours (white, canary, pink) for every menu. The HUD is one object: an adding-machine tape curling down the right edge that prints each loss and its causal chain, then tears off and flutters away. Type: one monospace, one stencil, one typewriter face.

AUDIO (from CC0 and royalty-free libraries, layered and pitched by the agent):
- Impacts: 12 material families x 3 sizes x 3 intensities, with debris tails (glass tinkle, brick clatter, steel ring).
- Structures speak before they fail: creaks, pings and groans 0.4-2.5 s ahead. Drama and information at once.
- The cat: real recorded meows, purrs, chirps, hisses and the hork wind-up; the purr doubles as the sub-bass of the mix.
- The Model: dot-matrix printer, stamp thunk, adding-machine crank, modem warble.
- Music: adaptive HOLD MUSIC. Calm play gets an insurer's bossa-nova hold loop; as chain depth rises it is pushed through tape wobble, distortion, breakbeats and brass in five stems; in the void it plays slowed and underwater; in rewilded districts it thins to solo guitar and birdsong.
- Humans do not speak: pictogram speech bubbles and short vocal reactions. No voice acting anywhere.

WHAT "AAA FEEL" MEANS HERE (measurable, so an AI agent can be held to it): 60 fps at 1080p on the target laptop and never under 45 in the largest collapse; input to reaction within one frame; nothing ever pops in or vanishes in view; every break has all four layers; the cat never slides, clips or snaps. Breadth of content is not on this list, and cannot be.
signature_moments: THE FIRST FOUR DOLLARS. A pint glass pushed off the bar, real shards, real spill, and an adding-machine tape printing 'GLASSWARE, 1 - TOTAL LOSS - $4.00'. The whole game in eight seconds.
MANHOLE POPCORN. One spark in a leaking gas main under Old Quay high street and twelve manhole covers launch 30 m into the air one after another down the road, each landing through a different roof.

THE EXCESS. A scratch-cut in the dam becomes a jet, the jet erodes a breach, and a wall of water takes 70 seconds to run the gorge to the sea; when it reaches the substation the night skyline goes dark block by block.

TOWER DOMINOES AND THE OAK. Cut one Surety tower on its east side, winch it with nine yarn lines anchored to the Old Oak, and fell it into its twin; the part that lands on the park is sliced clean in two by a tree that does not lose a leaf.
THE FLOATING ORCHARD. Excavate a whole park and every tree stays exactly where it was, hanging on its own plug of earth with roots dangling over a 10 m pit, birds still singing.

A VOLCANO IN THE LOBBY. Sixty metres of shaft dug straight down under the atrium of Solid Ground Tower; lava climbs it at walking pace, meets the aquifer on the way, and announces itself with a steam blast that takes out thirty floors of glass.
PULLING THE PLUG. A hole through the NO DATA crust, a trench to the harbour, and the sea drains out through the bottom of the world in a whirlpool, leaving the cargo ship sitting on mud.

RUNNING UP AN EXPLOSION. Freeze Frame half a second after the fireworks warehouse goes: climb the frozen fireball and its hanging debris like a staircase, land nine swats on a frozen container, step off, let time go.
THE BIG WHEEL. Cut two bearings and the 45 m Ferris wheel rolls off its stand, down the pier, through the arcade and into the sea, gondolas swinging.

OPEN DAY. Every zoo enclosure broken at once: two elephants stroll unbothered through a burning street, shouldering parked cars aside, while a giraffe looks into a third-floor office full of screaming accountants.

THE NORTH ARROW. Reaching the edge of the world for the first time and finding the map's own scale bar, legend and north arrow lying on the ground at full size, and discovering that the north arrow can be knocked off.
WALKING A FIRE WHIRL. Three laps of Zoomies around a burning petrol station and you are leading a 30 m pillar of fire down the main street on a leash.
IF I FITS, I SITS. A cat the size of a ferry settles onto the arena's cable roof, tucks her paws in, and the roof gives up one cable at a time.
THE SECOND TAKE. Watch a tower collapse, rewind it until it is standing, toss one fuel-soaked hairball into the lift shaft, let go, and watch a completely different collapse.
LIGHTING THE SUBWAY. Gas let into one station for two minutes, one spark at the far end, and all four station entrances exhale at the same instant while the street between them heaves and drops.
NINE CATS, ONE NOTE. Eight Echoes and you, all purring at exactly 0.3 Hz around the tallest tower in the city until it starts to sway like a reed.
PROXIMATE CAUSE: FLOWERPOT. The claim form at the end of an eleven-link accident you only half intended, listing every step from the windowsill to the tanker.
THE COMMUTING KOI. Break the glasshouse pond and each fish drifts away through the air inside its own wobbling ball of water, heading for the river.
THE QUIET AFTER. Downtown at dusk a day later: wild flowers over the rubble hills, deer on what was the bank plaza, fireflies, and a patch of catnip where the lobby used to be.
OFF THE TABLE. The final prompt: the whole city seen as a model on a ruled table, one paw, one push.
extra_ideas: A reaction table the director can edit: materials, thresholds and reactions live in one spreadsheet-like data file. Later it becomes the modding hook (new materials, new fluids) that keeps material-sandbox communities alive for years.

The Lab: a flat test range where any building, prop, fluid or animal can be spawned. It is the player's creative mode and, more importantly, the AI agent's automated test bench: headless runs that assert things like 'a 10-storey frame with two corner columns removed collapses within 8 s at 60 fps' catch regressions that no human is there to see.
Vertical slice before city: one Old Quay block, the bar interior, 64 m of ground and one world edge, with ten tools. Nothing else is built until that block meets the feel targets.

Event of the Week: a fixed seed, one district, ten minutes, a leaderboard for the biggest single chain, and the winning Timeline replay downloadable by everyone (replays are tiny: they are recordings of positions).

Clip-first features: an auto-generated claim-form image at the end of every chain (the causal list plus a screenshot), automatic before-and-after photo pairs of every landmark from the same camera position and, if the Steam plugin in use exposes it, markers on Steam's own recording timeline at every big chain.

Weather as a later peril you can summon: wind direction steers fire and gas (weather vanes show it), rain soaks wood and fills your pits, lightning strikes the tallest conductor (fly a wet yarn line from a tower), a heatwave lowers every ignition point.

Repair crews: districts that are damaged but not Written Off slowly get scaffolding, cranes and rebuilt floors. It stops half-wrecked areas going stale, and scaffolding is one of the best physics toys there is.
The Great Milk Flood: one tank in the tank farm and a few tankers carry milk, a white twin of water that every cat in the city converges on; flooding a street with it recruits your Colony.
Idle cat behaviour as charm and marketing: leave the controller alone and Rophe loafs, grooms, chatters at birds, kneads, and sits in any box-shaped piece of wreckage.

Comfort and access: Gentle Mode (humans only tumble), a photosensitivity mode that removes flashes and glitch strobing, sliders for camera shake and automatic slow motion, colour-blind-safe Model Vision palettes, full remapping, controller and handheld profiles.
A free demo built from the vertical slice: one block plus one edge, rank capped at 1-in-50. The edge discovery is the hook for streamers; the demo ends the first time the player falls off the world.
Stream integration later: chat votes on the next patch note, or bets on where the re-drop will land.
A second cat (local co-op) only after release: the simulation has one authority, and co-op doubles every budget.
risks: EXPECTATION GAP. 'AAA in every respect' is not reachable by a solo, zero-budget, AI-built project; AAA feel in the 30-second loop is. Agree the five measurable feel targets with the director up front, and gate everything on the one-block vertical slice: if it misses them, cut scope, never quality.

PERFORMANCE IN GDSCRIPT. Structural graphs, voxel meshing and the Field are all heavy, and every budget in this concept (1,200 awake bodies, 6,000 resting, 150-200 humans, 1 m cells at 10 Hz) is a target, not a measurement. Week-one benchmarks on the target laptop must decide: Field on a GPU compute shader or on worker threads; own voxel mesher or a prebuilt voxel-terrain extension; whether installing a C++ toolchain for one small native module is justified. The project must also leave the GL Compatibility renderer set in C:\Users\Cayan\Desktop\CatAsRophe\project.godot for the Forward+ renderer (compute shaders, global illumination, volumetrics).

FRACTURE PIPELINE WITHOUT BLENDER. Python mesh cutting will fail on some free kit meshes (open shells, overlapping parts). Fallback: fracture clean hidden structure proxies (plain slabs, beams, wall blocks) and let the pretty kit mesh ride on them as skin panels.

REWIND. It works only because it is a recording rather than a re-simulation, and it costs memory and CPU; fluids and fire reverse approximately and may show seams. Ship rigid-body and fracture rewind first, voxel edits second, Field rewind last; cap the window rather than fake it.

WATER THAT LOOKS LIKE CELLS. A 1 m fluid grid can look blocky. It needs a smoothed surface and foam shader; if that is not good enough, restrict free-flowing water to sheets and jets and treat large floods as rising level bodies.

ASSET COHERENCE AND THE 'ASSET FLIP' LOOK. The same free kits appear in many small games. The re-skin pipeline, the lighting and the Model's own identity are the answer, but an AI agent cannot reliably judge beauty: the director must review screenshot contact sheets at fixed checkpoints.

LICENCES. Sketchfab and itch.io assets vary file by file: CC-BY needs credit, NC and ND are unusable in a paid game, and some 'free' uploads are ripped from commercial games. CC0 first, a ledger for everything, reject anything with unclear origin. Same discipline for audio.

THE CAT'S ANIMATION. There is no animator, and free rigged cats with a full, good locomotion set are rare. Plan for procedural animation layers from the start; this is the largest single threat to 'feel'.

'EVERYTHING BREAKS' IS TESTED IN MINUTE ONE. A single unbreakable chair breaks the spell. Add an automated check that fails the build if any man-made object lacks a material tag, fracture data and an insured value.

TONE AND RATING. Harming humans is in the brief; the paper treatment and Gentle Mode keep it comic, but store copy, trailers and age-rating questionnaires need care, and nothing should reward hurting crowds as such.

SYSTEMS OVERLOAD. Sixteen materials and seven stimuli are a lot to learn. Introduce them in stages (the bar teaches four), and lean on Model Vision, Claims Book silhouettes and the legend lying at the edge of the world.

PHYSICS FAILURES AT THE BEST MOMENTS. Jitter, tunnelling, exploding stacks and frame-time spikes arrive exactly when the spectacle peaks. Conservative body budgets, the chaos governor's slow motion and falling clusters (few big bodies instead of many small ones) are the defences.

THEME RISKS. The joke rests on English insurance jargon ('cat' = catastrophe) and the title pun is English-only: it needs a one-line in-game explanation and careful localisation. The Model's deliberate artefacts must never read as real bugs (keep them crisp, designed, and always paired with the paper-rustle cue). The invented names (the insurer, the districts) need a clearance search before release.

TWENTY TOOLS IS A LOT TO BUILD. First playable ships ten (Swat and Pounce, Claws, Scruff, Dig, Meow, Hairball, Zoomies sprint, Rewind, slow motion, Replay); the rest are added in the order in which they exercise new systems.

SAVE ROBUSTNESS. A ten-hour destroyed world is precious and the file format will change during development: versioning, migration and backups from the first save, and a size cap that is actually enforced.

UNVERIFIED FACTS AND ONE REAL COST. Web search was unavailable in this session (search budget exhausted), so statements about engine features, plugins, Steam features (Auto-Cloud, the recording timeline) and asset licences come from memory and must be checked in the week-one spike. Releasing on Steam also carries a per-app submission fee (about US$100, from memory), the one cost a zero budget cannot avoid.

sources.caveats: VERDICT: USE (backbone). About 215 GB in total and each library is only a sample selection. The zip part holding a given library is undocumented: choose files from the CSV track lists, download that year, extract the picks, delete the rest. The licence version published on the download day governs: archive a dated copy of https://sonniss.com/gdc-bundle-license/. Never commit the WAVs to a public repo or ship them as loose files; keep them inside the exported PCK. Only the first 100-200k characters of each track list were read, so more relevant libraries exist. The 2026 bundle has no cat, earthquake or large-explosion content.

Scriptable route (verified): the Godot Asset Library API returns GitHub commit zips of CC0 mirrors - Impact Sounds id 1841 (https://github.com/Loppansson/kenney-impact-sounds-for-godot), Sci-Fi Sounds 1834, Digital Audio 1833 (https://github.com/Loppansson/kenney-digital-audio-for-godot), UI Audio 796 (https://github.com/Calinou/kenney-ui-audio), Interface Sounds 794, RPG Audio 1840, Music Jingles 1839, Particle Pack 784 (https://github.com/Calinou/kenney-particle-pack), Input Prompts 2655 (https://github.com/tanuki-billie/kenney-input-prompts, v1.1, older than the site's 1.5a), Prototype Textures 781.
