concept_world.concept_name: CAT AS ROPHE - The Lease Is Up (design codename: STET)
concept_world.one_line_pitch: A slapstick 3D demolition sandbox in which a stray cat turns out to be the eleven-years-overdue undo command for a fake showroom town: knock everything humans staged off the table, from wine glasses to skyscrapers to the bedrock, and the more you wreck, the wilder and more beautiful the real valley underneath becomes.
concept_world.style_answer:
Short answer: not a pixel sandbox. Build a hybrid: real 3D models with mesh fracture for everything man-made, a smooth voxel ground for the strata, and a pixel-sandbox brain (a small table of material rules) driving both. The look is Brochure Hyperreal.

Option 1 - 2D falling-sand pixel sandbox. Strength: every pixel is a material, so fire, water and collapse combine by themselves. Verdict: rejected. It contradicts four hard requirements at once (3D open world, climbable buildings, real 3D models, AAA feel) and turns the cat into a 12-pixel sprite. Keep its idea, not its look: about 16 materials times 6 forces (impact, weight, heat, water, electricity, sound) with one simple rule per pair, so chain reactions emerge instead of being scripted.

Option 2 - full 3D voxel world. Strength: one rule for everything, cut anything anywhere, digging is free. Verdict: rejected as the base. (a) To look good, voxels must be about 10 cm; a 1.6 km map is then tens of billions of cells and needs a custom native engine, which this production cannot build (GDScript only, no C/C++ toolchain). (b) Free models from Kenney, Sketchfab or itch.io would have to be voxelised and would lose exactly the real-model look that was asked for. (c) Cubes read as indie-blocky rather than AAA, and the game would be judged directly against the best-known voxel destruction and block-building games.

Option 3 - hybrid (recommended).
- Man-made things are real meshes, pre-cut at build time by a Python pipeline into three sizes (element 1-6 m, chunk 0.3-1.5 m, crumb 5-30 cm) with proper inside faces (rebar, brick core, insulation), held together by a support graph so buildings fail the way structures fail.
- The ground is a smooth voxel volume (0.5 m cells, 48 m deep, generated only where the player digs or blasts), so asphalt, fill, soil, clay, aquifer and rock are real layers.
- The bridge between the two is what makes it feel new: settled debris is never deleted. The bottom of every pile fuses into rubble ground, so broken buildings literally become terrain that can be dug, climbed and that later grows over.
- It fits the machine: with Jolt physics and the Forward+ renderer the design budget is about 2,000 moving bodies plus tens of thousands of resting ones drawn in batches, at 1080p and 60 fps.

Brochure Hyperreal: the town is rendered like a real-estate brochure (golden light, slightly too clean, too saturated, people who smile too evenly); not photoreal, not cartoon. Three reasons. It is achievable with free assets, because the pipeline re-skins every downloaded model with one house library of about 12 PBR materials, which is what makes mixed sources look like one world. It makes destruction read: raw concrete, rebar and dust against a spotless brochure is maximum contrast. And it is the fiction: the town is a sales showroom. The simulation layer gets its own original identity (paper, ink and a proofreader's red pencil; see edge_of_world) instead of green code on black.
concept_world.story:
FOUR FRAMINGS, ONE VERDICT
A. The cat realises it lives in a simulation and tears it down (director). Keeps: explains the edge, the void, the re-drop, rewind and why nothing can kill you. Problems: the awakened rebel is the most-used simulation plot there is; it makes the cat angry and purposeful, which is less funny than a cat being a cat; and it puts a realisation before the fun.
B. Psychedelic candy in a bar (prototype). Keeps: a great first image (stray, bar, glowing treat). Problems: 'it was a trip' means nothing you do matters, it cannot explain the simulated edge or the nature rule, and drug framing buys rating friction for no gain.
C. Small god of knocked-over things on its ninth life (my discard). Charming, explains invulnerability, has no room for the simulation edge, which is a hard requirement.
D. The Undo (my pick, built from A and B). The cat does not rebel against the simulation. The cat IS the simulation's own long-overdue undo command, delivered inside a glowing treat behind a bar, running in the body of a stray because that is the one kind of thing the town's management cannot refuse, stop or delete. The player, not the cat, has the realisation, at the edge of the world.

THE TRUTH OF THE WORLD (never told in one piece; found)
- First there was the Survey: a naturalist's life work, a perfect living record of one coastal valley, every tree, animal, root and stream, stored on a rented world-host. Everything in it is filed AS IS: real, protected, not to be altered by anyone.
- Then the host leased the space above it. A property developer built a showroom town on top to pre-sell homes: Vellum Bay, A Planned Community. It drowned a grove under a reservoir, buried the meadow under 4 to 8 m of fill and staged the streets with 1,204 smiling Residents (12 faces between them).
- No buyer ever came. The developer vanished. The lease expired 4,015 days ago. The town's automated caretaker, The Management, has kept the lights on and announced OPEN HOUSE TOMORROW every day since.
- The lease says expired land must be returned as found by a standard job: Rollback Of Persistent Human Edits, ROPHE. For eleven years The Management has refused the job at the door.
- The world's entire code is one kind of sentence: [what a thing really is] AS [what it is presented as]. FACADE AS HOUSE. LOOP_03 AS NEIGHBOUR. JPEG AS MOUNTAINS. Real things are filed as themselves: OAK AS OAK, HERON AS HERON.
- The Surveyor (the naturalist, preserved in his own survey, the only real person in the valley) finds the loophole: The Management cannot refuse, stop or remove an animal. So he files the job as one: RUN ROPHE AS CAT. He hides it in a treat for the stray he feeds behind the bar. A late margin note admits he named the job after the cat and worked the acronym backwards.
So the title is three lines of the world's own code, one per act: ROPHE AS CAT (what the paperwork claims: a job dressed as a cat), CAT AS ROPHE (what is actually happening: a real cat doing the job, a catastrophe), CAT AS CAT (what is left when the job is done).

WHO ROPHE IS
A lean tuxedo stray, about 4.5 kg, tipped left ear, amber eyes, no collar. Not a hero, not a rebel, never angry, never speaks, understands none of the above. The treat did one thing: it made everything man-made knockable. All comedy is ordinary cat behaviour at disaster scale: the look straight at a witness before pushing the thing off the edge, the loaf, the zoomies, the 'I meant to do that' groom after a bus lands on you.

THE ONE RULE
Living things are AS IS. That single rule covers three requirements: you cannot harm plants or animals; The Management cannot harm you; you cannot die. The cat's immunity and the pigeon's immunity are the same law, shown with the same effect.

WHO THE HUMANS ARE
Staging. Residents are showroom props running daily loops and speaking brochure. They are not people; knocked out, they fold flat into a labelled cardboard box that The Management re-assembles later. One deliberate, removable exception: the Surveyor, an old gardener on a bench at Lot 000 in the park, cannot be boxed. Hit him and you get the same mark as a tree. He tips his hat.

WHO RUNS IT
Nobody. That is the joke and the sadness. No villain at a console, no outside world shown; the Host stopped answering long ago and only its billing still runs. What remains: two leftover routines (The Management, and the job inside the cat), one real man, and a blank page beyond the map. The Management is the antagonist: a relentlessly polite notice-writer with no face and no voice, only signs.

HOW THE WORLD REACTS (four acts, driven by global Rollback percent)
- Act I, 0-15, 'Pets must be supervised': denial. Residents step around craters; Tidy Crews tape things up.
- Act II, 15-40, 'Scheduled maintenance': Animal Control, nets, laser-dot decoys, sprinklers. Each dawn wrecked blocks are re-staged as cardboard facades. Price boards fall. Residents' loops break.
- Act III, 40-70, 'Budget reallocation': to pay for repairs The Management stops paying for detail. Standing buildings lose their textures and turn into white model-board, the muzak skips, Residents return as cheaper copies, wildlife moves into the ruins.
- Act IV, 70-99, 'Final notice': a white paper town in a green valley. What is left of the Sales Tower stands up on crane legs and tries to walk off the map with the lease.
- 100: everything man-made still standing unspools into the sky as loose sheets. The valley is whole.

ENDINGS
1. CAT AS CAT (stay): the tag over the cat is corrected in red pencil and marked 'stet' (let it stand). Walk to the bench, press to sit on a lap. Credits over a living valley, then endless Valley Mode.
2. CAT AS ROPHE (again): sit in the middle of the town's scale model. The town is re-staged around everything that has grown. Lease 2 begins in the next season.
3. NOTHING AS YET (secret, needs all 9 lease Clauses): walk off the edge and do not fall. Each paw print on the blank page sprouts grass. The destroyer leaves as the first author of somewhere new.

HOW MUCH STORY UP FRONT, AND HOW IT IS TOLD
Open with story, but only 80 playable, skippable seconds with zero exposition; the game never says the word simulation. After that, control is never taken for more than 5 seconds. Everything is carried by things you pass at full sprint: printed notices (The Management), handwritten margin notes (the Surveyor), AS labels, property price boards, what is buried underground, what the edge shows, and 9 short lease Clauses. A player who never reads a word still gets the arc: a fake town falls, a real valley returns, a cat goes home.

TONE, NO DEATH, PERSISTENCE, RESET
Three parts deadpan slapstick to one part quiet wonder. Never grim, gory or cruel; the darkest note is a showroom that waited eleven years for guests. No health bar and no game over: the worst outcome is embarrassment (soaked, netted, driven to the Pound in a carrier, which you then demolish from inside). The world is fully persistent. 'Reset the simulation' exists inside the fiction as Re-staging (see save_system).
concept_world.intro_sequence:
Length: 80 seconds from title to free roam, player in control from second 12. Skippable at any moment (hold Esc or Start for 0.8 s: jump to the bar front blowing out, already in control). On later new games and re-stages it shortens itself to 6 seconds. No narration, no text crawl, no explanation of the simulation.

0:00 The title is the first shot of the game, not a menu over black. Night, rain just ended, an alley behind a bar called The Tipsy Sardine, a tuxedo cat asleep on a crate, neon in the puddles. Brochure lettering reads ROPHE AS CAT; small line beneath: 'Vellum Bay - Open House Tomorrow'. A red pencil draws the proofreader's transpose mark (the curve that means swap these two words) around ROPHE and CAT. The printing plates slip with a paper-jam crunch and the title becomes CAT AS ROPHE; small line: 'a catastrophe sandbox'. The director's gag is kept, drawn in the game's own visual language, and it plants the seed that pays off at the edge of the world.
0:06 Press any key. No cut: the camera sinks from the title framing to behind the cat. Rophe wakes and stretches. A food bowl with ROPHE written on it in marker. Through the open back door: warm light, muzak, five Residents repeating the same 6-second toast and the same laugh. Slightly wrong, never explained.
0:12 Control. A fish-shaped treat glowing vermilion lands in the bowl with a rubber-stamp thunk. A hand-inked arrow fades off the wall: 'for you'. (The prototype's glowing candy in a bar, now with a job to do.)
0:20 Eat. Pupils blow wide. For one second every man-made object in view gets a faint red-pencil underline; the pigeon on the windowsill gets a row of dots instead. The muzak skips once.
0:30 The bar counter. The only tutorial line in the intro: 'Knock it off.' The first wine glass slides, tips, falls and shatters at 30 percent speed. The bartender keeps polishing: 'Lovely evening!' Second glass: his loop stutters. Hold to grab a bottle and throw it at the back shelf: 40 bottles, the mirror and the shelf come down. A falling keg bonks a Resident, who folds flat into a cardboard box printed RESIDENT (1) with a carry handle. First laugh; the human rule is taught without a word.
0:50 'Hold to Yowl.' The front wall and windows blow out into the street. The camera pulls back to play distance and tilts up: skyline, the 96 m Sales Tower, its screen reading OPEN HOUSE TOMORROW. In the middle of the glass storm a pigeon stands on the kerb, untouched, pecking. The nature rule is taught in the first minute, as a joke.
1:10 A printed notice slaps onto the nearest lamp post: 'The Management reminds residents that pets must be supervised.' The HUD fades in (one ring, nine pips). Free roam; everything in sight breaks.

What the player knows after 80 seconds without being told: swat, grab and throw, yowl; everything breaks at every scale from glass to wall; people fold into boxes; animals are untouchable; someone polite is annoyed; something about this town is off.
concept_world.core_loop:
The verb of the game is: knock it off. Three nested loops.

10 seconds - Swat. See a thing, push it, watch honest physics, hear it. Every fragment produced is immediately a new toy: ammunition, a step, a wedge.

5 to 10 minutes - The Job, at one landmark.
1. Scout: flick on Cat's Eye (night vision plus the AS labels). It shows what is load-bearing, what each thing is made of, where gas, water and power run under the street, and the sepia ghost of any Suppressed Giant tree the building sits on.
2. Rig: combine two or three tools. Yarn two towers together, send Clockwork Mice to the columns, dig under a corner, plant a Catgrass seed in the lobby, glue up a wrecking ball.
3. Trigger, then savour: Slow Blink through it, Stare to freeze and rearrange it in mid-air, Take-Back to do it differently, Encore to film it.
4. Aftermath: the rubble stays and becomes terrain. Within 30 seconds green pushes through. The district price board drops (FROM 450,000 to FROM 12). The Management answers with a notice and new moving targets (vans, cranes, a helicopter), which are more things to break. A crow circles the next Treat.

About an hour - A district is Returned. At 85 percent of its original standing mass down, The Management writes the district off; the remainder turns white and overgrows by itself, a Giant or three erupt, wildlife moves in, the muzak there dies and birdsong replaces it. Global Rollback moves, the act changes, the whole map reacts.

Fuel: Mischief, one ring on the HUD. It fills from variety and causality, not volume. A new material, a new object type and each link in a chain reaction (A cut B, which lit C, which dropped D) score more than the last; repeating the same act scores less each time. Mischief pays for the big verbs (Zoomies 25, Table Rule 40, Puff Up 100), so the loop quietly teaches players to build chain reactions instead of spamming one attack.

There is no fail state. Being caught by Animal Control is a free ride across the map in a carrier you can burst at any moment.
concept_world.world_design:
Vellum Bay is a coastal showroom town on a square slab floating in the Margin.
- Slab: 1,600 x 1,600 m (2.56 square km), 48 m thick. Finished town: about 1,200 m across. Outer 150-250 m: unfinished Phase 2 and the edge. Sea level 0 m, downtown +6 m, the Heights up to +85 m, reservoir surface +52 m. Tallest structure: Sales Tower, 96 m.
- Scale check: a sprint (13 m/s) crosses the town in about 90 seconds, Zoomies in 45. Small enough that every block is hand-tuned and persistent; big enough that the far skyline is a promise. From any tower top you see the whole slab and, at night, a pale false dawn on every horizon: the Margin glowing. That glow is what first pulls players to the edge.
- A river runs north to south: reservoir, dam, park, downtown, the Old Quarter canal, the bay. Five bridges. A monorail loop (2.4 km, 6 stations) and a ring road supply moving targets. A day lasts 24 minutes (16 light, 8 dark).
- Near the player: up to 300 Residents, 120 vehicles, about 40 animated animals plus bird flocks.

Eight districts, each with one landmark, one destruction fantasy and one signature chain reaction.
1. Sardine Row (Old Quarter, south centre, 250 x 250 m, start). Brick, timber, tile, a covered market, the canal, the 38 m Clock Tower. Fantasy: tactile, brick-by-brick breakage at cat scale. Chain: fell the Clock Tower along the high street; its 3-tonne bell rolls downhill through the market into the canal.
2. Prospect Square (Downtown, centre, 300 x 300 m). Six glass-and-steel towers of 40 to 96 m, the Sales Tower with a 30 m screen, the Sales Office lobby with a scale model of the whole town. Fantasy: felling skyscrapers. Chain: tower-into-tower dominoes; a curtain wall shedding 2,000 panes floor by floor.
3. The Galleria and Showhome Mile (west centre, 350 x 300 m). A mall with a glass atrium, a 6-level car park, the flat-pack megastore Plank and Peg, the Fine China Emporium. Fantasy: the indoor rampage. Chain: car park pancake (6 slabs, 400 cars, every alarm), and 4,000 pieces of porcelain in one room.
4. Pleasant Loop (suburb, north-west, 450 x 400 m). 80 near-identical showhomes on a spiral cul-de-sac, a 32 m water tower, a school, a barbecue that never ends. Fantasy: dominoes and repetition. Chain: the gas-main zipper (one spark runs the street house by house), then the water tower puts it out and floods the loop.
5. Cannery Quay and the Pier (south-east, 400 x 300 m). Three 55 m gantry cranes, the container ship MV Open House, 8 fuel tanks, the Bay Sardine Co. cannery, a substation, a pier with a 45 m Ferris wheel, a coaster and a fireworks barge. Fantasy: industrial chain reactions. Chain: crane onto ship, 600 containers cascade, fuel farm, fireworks finale; the Ferris wheel cut loose rolls the length of the boardwalk.
6. Belvedere Heights (north-east hills, 400 x 400 m). Villas on stilts, a cable car, an observatory, a 110 m guyed radio mast, five 70 m wind turbines. Fantasy: gravity; whatever you break here arrives somewhere else. Chain: cut one guy wire; snap the cable-car line; bowl a turbine rotor downhill into Downtown.
7. Stillwater Dam (north, 400 x 350 m). A 46 m concrete arch dam with a 220 m crest, a hydro plant, the reservoir. Fantasy: the biggest single domino on the map. Chain: breach it and a flood wave runs the river through park, downtown and Old Quarter to the bay in about 70 seconds; the drained reservoir reveals a drowned grove of standing, untouchable trees.
8. Common Ground (park, north centre, 350 x 300 m). The only nature the brochure allowed: lawns, a pond with a heron, a bandstand where the same wedding happens every day at 14:00, a 60 m glass Palm House, the Zoo and Aquarium, and Lot 000 - NOT FOR SALE: a scruffy wild corner with a shed, a bench and the Surveyor. Fantasy: liberation. Break every cage, tank and pane; nothing alive is hurt; an elephant walks out through the mall. Lot 000 is home.

Edge ring: Phase 2 facades to the west and north-west, flat cut-out mountains behind the reservoir, and to the south and east a sea that pours silently off the side of the world (see edge_of_world). The underground is a ninth district laid under all the others (see ground_layers).

Build order: one vertical slice first (Sardine Row, one 40 m tower, a 30 m strip of edge, one 48 m dig column) polished to final quality before any other district is started.
concept_world.ground_layers:
The slab is 48 m thick. Every layer is a real voxel material with its own strength, sound and behaviour. The whole stack is drawn in labelled cross-section on the cut face of the world's edge, which is how players learn it is there. Depths are below the local street.

1. Finish, 0-0.3 m. Asphalt, pavers, tile. Cracks into plates, peels in sheets, softens to tar near fire. First thing through every crack: green.
2. Slab and base, 0.3-1.5 m. Reinforced concrete road slab, crushed stone, kerbs; building footings and basements reach down to 8 m. Do: Pounce from height or Loaf to punch through; dig under a footing and that corner of the building sinks.
3. Services, 1.5-4 m. Colour-coded mains: water (blue), gas (yellow), power and fibre (red), plus storm drains and sewers big enough to run through, the cat motorway under the town; rats show the way. Do: start chain reactions from below: geysers that lift cars, gas jets, district blackouts.
4. Made Ground, 'the Changelog', 4-8 m. The town was rebuilt on top of its own earlier versions. Three buried builds: v3 (older branding; the town was called Parchment Point), v2 (a flat-shaded low-poly town; the kit models already in the prototype's asset folder belong here), v1 (a grey-box street of 1.5 m cubes that pop into four small cubes and vanish after three seconds: the first prototype itself, kept as archaeology, with a notice: 'Debris removal after 3 seconds was discontinued following feedback.' It is the only place in the game where debris ever disappears). Find: Treats, deprecated props, a time capsule. This layer also turns the unavoidable style mix of free asset packs into fiction.
5. The Seedbed, 8-9 m. The valley's original topsoil, black and full of dormant seed. Open it to daylight with a pit 3 m wide and it sprouts in 30 seconds. The Surveyor's first note is written here: 'there you are.'
6. Subsoil and clay, 9-16 m. Stiff, waterproof, holds any shape you carve. The roots of the 40 Suppressed Giants hang here as untouchable, faintly glowing lattices: natural tunnel props and ladders. Mole, rabbit and fox burrows are ready-made passages; a mole will lead you to the nearest Giant.
7. Aquifer, 16-22 m. Water-bearing sand and gravel. It flows at a 32 degree slope and tunnels do not hold unless roots carry them. Dig below the water table and your workings flood up to 14 m below the street. An underground stream is a water slide to an outfall in the sea cliff. Breach the aquifer under a building and you have made a sinkhole. Water brought down from here is the key to layer 10.
8. Bedrock, 22-38 m. Bedded limestone; needs Purr, Pounce or Clockwork Mice before claws work. Three caverns: the Bat Vault, the Still Lake, and Leviathan Hall, where a 40 m fossil skeleton is filed AS IS: you cannot break it, only excavate around it, and uncovering all of it is one of the game's quiet goals. Loose boulders are 20-tonne ammunition worth hauling up.
9. Rock (Assumed), 38-43 m. The survey never went this deep, so the world stops being measured and becomes a guess: paper-white rock drawn in pen hatching, labelled LIMESTONE (ASSUMED) and DEPTH UNKNOWN, with a note: 'nobody checked. - S.' It weighs almost nothing and digs like foam board; the sound turns to pencil on paper.
10. Magma (Assumed), 43-46 m. A slow, hand-inked, lava-lamp orange. The system has no rule for a protected cat touching guessed magma, so it rejects you: you are fired 60 m back up your own shaft like a cork. (The prototype's lava bounce, kept and made useful: exit, then Pounce from the top.) To pass, bring water: cut a shaft so the aquifer, the river or the reservoir drains onto it. Result: a steam blast that turns your shaft into a geyser cannon, and a 1 m crust labelled OBSIDIAN (PROBABLY). Break the crust.
11. The Underside, 46-48 m. The last sheet: grey pulp board stamped with the lot number and lease Clause 8, GROUND AS GIVEN. Break through and daylight-white pours in.

Below the last layer: nothing as yet. You fall out of the bottom of the world into the Margin, the same blank, luminous page that lies beyond the edges. Looking up as you fall you see the slab from underneath: Giant roots hanging like chandeliers, the developer's piles bolted on with barcodes, the sea from below with fish swimming over the void. Then the edge rule applies: the page returns you from the sky at a random spot. The deepest thing claws can do is dig through the planet and come back as a meteor.
concept_world.edge_of_world:
Original visual identity: this simulation does not look like green code on black. Its code is paperwork. The world is a marked-up printer's proof in three hands: Print (The Management's plotter-blue lines and brochure type), Ink (the Surveyor's sepia handwriting and watercolour) and Red Pencil (the cat's corrections: delete loops, 'stet' dots, transpose curves). The void is the Margin: warm, bright, backlit paper white, not darkness. The code artefacts are AS labels: small typeset tags on thin leader lines reading [what it is] AS [what it plays].

Step by step, walking west from town (the edge is 800 m from the centre):
1. Lure, from anywhere at night: a pale false dawn on every horizon.
2. 250 m from the edge, 'Phase 2 - Coming Soon'. Hoardings, then houses that are only fronts propped with timber. One car model with one number plate, parked 30 times. Residents with the same face on 3-second loops. The city's background sound audibly loops every 8 seconds, with a click. Lawns are painted floor. Animals, by contrast, look sharper and more alive the further out you go; a fox trots through, perfectly real.
3. 180 m, the Peel. Colour comes off buildings in sheets that curl upward and drift away like wet posters, leaving matte white model-board. Shadows become pen hatching. The sky shows printer's marks: crop marks in its corners, a colour bar along the horizon, clouds slightly out of register.
4. 120 m, the Labels. Tags fade in on everything: FACADE AS HOUSE. LOOP_03 AS NEIGHBOUR. PAINT AS LAWN. JPEG AS MOUNTAINS. FALLBACK AS SKY. In sepia handwriting: FOX AS FOX. From now on labels can be seen anywhere through Cat's Eye.
5. 60 m, the Draft. Model-board thins to pencil outlines with dimension arrows ('12.50 m'). The road is two ruled lines: ROAD AS INTENDED. Placeholder cubes: BOX AS YET. Facades here are free-standing sheets: one swat and forty house fronts go down like dominoes into the white.
6. First visit only, the mirror. A last shop window (or a puddle) reflects the cat with a tag over its head: ROPHE AS CAT. Rophe paws at it. A red pencil draws the transpose mark and the words swap: CAT AS ROPHE. The title was a line of this world's code all along. Five seconds, no dialogue, the camera stays the player's. A notice lands: 'The Management has been made aware of an unauthorised process running as a cat.'
7. The edge itself. The ground stops like a cut sheet. On the cut face the full 48 m of strata is drawn as a labelled cross-section (ASPHALT AS ROAD, FILL AS GROUND, the buried older towns, ROCK (ASSUMED), MAGMA (ASSUMED)): the game's advertisement for digging. To the south and east the sea slides over the edge without a sound and breaks into ink-wash droplets. Far out in the white hang huge pale words, NOTHING AS YET, and, tiny in the distance, other slabs with their own tags: LOT 2: ALPINE AS RESORT. LOT 3: REEF AS MARINA.
8. The fall. Step off, get thrown off or drive off. No damage. Fall speed is capped at 30 m/s and you steer by spreading your paws. You pass the cross-section, then the underside of the slab.
9. The void, 12 seconds. White in every direction, pencil-scratch room tone instead of wind. You fall between enormous translucent sheets: first the developer's blue plan of the town, then beneath it the Surveyor's watercolour map of the valley as it was before the town: a preview of what you are restoring.
10. The re-drop. Half a second of pure white, then you are 350 m above a random point of the map, chosen with a 70 percent bias toward places you have not yet wrecked. You can steer about 150 m, you land on your feet, and the landing is a Pounce: a crater scaled to the fall. A handwritten lost-property tag flicks past: 'found: one cat. returned to: Cannery Quay.' Step-off to landing takes about 22 seconds; after the first time, hold a button to fast-fall in 5.

Three consequences that make the edge a toy instead of a wall:
- The void deletes nothing. A bus, a boxed Resident or a tower top thrown off the edge falls out of the sky somewhere random about 20 seconds later.
- The sea that pours off the edge comes back as rain. After the dam breaks it rains for a day, and rain speeds regrowth.
- The edge creeps inward. From Act III The Management saves budget by peeling still-standing buildings to model-board, district by district, so a player who never walks to the border still meets the simulation, and the mirror beat can fire at any reflective surface inside a peeled zone.
concept_world.destruction_model:
Principle: conservation. Nothing man-made is ever deleted, only changed: element to chunk to crumb to rubble ground to green hill. A stats line says it out loud: 'Tonnes still on the map: 100 percent.'

WHAT BREAKS HOW
- Buildings are not solid models. Each is assembled from structural elements with true thickness (columns, beams, floor slabs, wall panels, glazing, cladding, stairs) plus furniture and props inside. Free downloaded models are used for dressing, vehicles, props, people and animals; hero buildings are built from the element kit so they can fail properly.
- Three sizes of breakage. Element (1-6 m) detaches from the structure. Chunk (0.3-1.5 m, 6-20 per element, pre-cut per material with correct inside faces) is the grab-and-throw size. Crumb (5-30 cm) is drawn as colliding particles and accounted for by volume as rubble and dust.
- Vehicles: panels dent and crumple, then tear off (doors, bonnet, wheels, glass, engine block); a burning tank explodes after 4 seconds; tyres roll a long way.
- Props (about 300 types): each has a material and one comedy behaviour (hydrants geyser, vending machines spray cans, pianos play a chord, shopping trolleys roll forever).
- Roads and ground: voxel layers; craters, trenches, tunnels, sinkholes and slumps.

MATERIAL TABLE (density in kg per cubic metre; toughness 1-10; how it fails; special)
- Glass: 2,500; 1; radial shatter from the hit point; tempered glass dices, laminated webs and sags in its frame; answers a high Yowl.
- Ceramic and tile: 2,300; 1; sharp shards; the best sound in the game.
- Plasterboard: 700; 1; punches through (cat-shaped holes at Zoomies speed); white dust.
- Timber: 600; 3; splinters along the grain; burns, chars, floats.
- Brick masonry: 1,900; 4; fails along the mortar into single bricks and clusters; a brick is the perfect throwable.
- Plain concrete and block: 2,300; 5; angular chunks, gravel, heavy grey dust.
- Reinforced concrete: 2,500; 7; cracks first, the cover spalls, chunks dangle on bent rebar before dropping.
- Structural steel: 7,850; 9; never shatters; bends at joints and tears at bolts; loses 60 percent of its strength in fire, so fire fells steel frames.
- Sheet metal: 2,700-7,800; 4; crumples and peels in panels; conducts Static.
- Asphalt: 2,300; 3; plates and sheets; sticky tar when hot.
- Plastic and rubber: 1,000; 2; bounces; melts.
- Paper, card, fabric, model-board: 50-700; 0.5; tears, flutters, burns fast, slumps when wet. Re-staged facades and late-game peeled buildings are this, so the endgame falls fast.
- Soil and fill: 1,600; 2; digs by paw; slumps at 40 degrees; mud when wet.
- Clay: 1,900; 4; holds vertical cuts; waterproof.
- Sand and gravel: 1,700; 1; flows at 32 degrees.
- Limestone: 2,600; 8; splits along its beds into slabs and boulders.
- Living things: not a material. AS IS.
Six forces act on these (impact, sustained weight, heat, water, electricity, sound), one simple rule per pair.

STRUCTURAL COLLAPSE RULES
1. Support. Every element must trace a path of intact joints to the ground. After any break the building re-checks; whatever is cut off becomes one falling cluster, which breaks along its joints on impact.
2. Overload. Each column and wall carries the mass above it. Over 100 percent of capacity it cracks and groans (a 1-3 second warning, with dust); over 130 percent it buckles and hands its load to its neighbours. That is progressive collapse: the right four columns bring down a tower.
3. Lean. If the weight above a storey sits more than 15 percent outside what still supports it, the top hinges and topples toward the missing side. Felling direction is a skill: cut the side you want it to fall to.
4. Impact. A falling floor adds its mass to the next; pancakes accelerate.
5. Rebar and bolts. Up to 300 broken reinforced-concrete and steel joints at a time become tethers that let chunks dangle and swing for 5-60 seconds.
6. Pacing. Collapse travels at most 12 storeys per second with 60-150 ms between breaks, so it reads, sounds right and never happens as one pop.
7. Distance. Sound travels at 343 m/s: you see the far tower go, then hear it.

DEBRIS LIFECYCLE (the answer to 'it vanished after 3 seconds')
1. Live: a simulated body. Budget about 2,000 at once; new fragments queue at up to 250 per frame.
2. Settled: at rest for 2 seconds it freezes in place at no physics cost, but stays an individual object you can grab, throw, climb or knock loose. Tens of thousands can exist.
3. Heaped: when a pile gets deep (over about 120 chunks in a 4 m cell) or has been far from the player for a minute, its buried bottom fuses into rubble ground of the same volume and colour. The top layer stays loose. Rubble ground can be dug, cratered and thrown.
4. Overgrown: after one or two dawns moss, ivy and saplings take it. Your first-hour buildings are your tenth-hour hills.
Dust hangs for 20-40 seconds, then settles as a visible layer that only rain or flood washes off. Things thrown off the map fall back out of the sky. Tidy Crews sweep rubble into skips: they move it, they never delete it. All of it is written to the save.

CHAIN REACTIONS (authored sources, emergent results)
- Gas: a cut main jets fire; a spark runs the street house by house.
- Fuel: cars have a 4-second fuse; a propane bottle becomes a rocket; the fuel farm takes the quay.
- Power: a tripped substation blacks out a district; fallen lines arc and start fires; Static rides metal for up to 9 hops.
- Water: hydrants lift cars; the water tower floods the suburb; the dam floods the river corridor; water shorts power, quenches fire, turns soil to mud and unlocks the magma.
- Height: everything on the Heights rolls downhill into something else.
- Dominoes: facades, pylons, cranes, turbines, towers.
- Undermining: remove the ground and the structure above obeys rule 1.
Chains are counted link by link, and links are what fill Mischief.

tools_and_powers.name: Paw: Swat, Scruff and Throw
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Innate. Tap to swat: a precise shove at the paw, from 300 N-s (one glass) to 6,000 N-s when charged for 1.2 s (a parked car off a pier). Hold to scruff: a red-pencil loop lifts any loose man-made piece, from 2 t with an empty Mischief ring up to 40 t with a full one (a loaded bus); aim, charge and throw at up to 60 m/s. Up to 5 pieces can orbit the cat and be fired in turn. Boxed Residents count as pieces.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: The knock-it-off-the-table verb scaled from wine glass to bus. It turns every fragment the game ever produces into ammunition, a step or a wedge.

tools_and_powers.name: Claws Out (climbing)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Innate. Rophe sticks to and runs up any man-made surface, including overhangs and ceilings, with no stamina meter; wall-jumps 6 m; hangs from ledges. Claws leave permanent scratch marks and shred soft materials (fabric, plasterboard, timber) on the way. Sheet glass is the exception: you slide down it with a screech unless you break it. Trees and ivy are climbable and are never marked.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Every building is a route and an inspection of its own weak points, and nothing beats climbing a tower while it is coming down.

tools_and_powers.name: Yarn (tether and climbing aid)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found in Purl, the wool shop on Sardine Row. Fires a strand up to 60 m. Grapple, swing and zip-line; tie any two things together (each strand holds 20 t, stretches 30 percent, 9 strands at once) and reel in to drag them toward each other. Strung between two trees, which cannot break, it becomes a giant slingshot or a tripwire that derails the monorail.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Rope physics for choosing where a tower falls, towing, catapults and a cat's-cradle snare across a whole street. Also the fastest way to cross town.

tools_and_powers.name: Dig and Litter Kick
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Innate. Dig burrows a 1.2 m tunnel through the ground layers (soil 3 m/s, clay 1.2 m/s, sand 4 m/s but it slumps, rock only after it has been cracked). The spoil is real and sprays out behind you. Litter Kick is the back-leg kick: a shotgun cone of whatever you are standing on (gravel, broken glass, rubble) that also buries up to 3 cubic metres per kick.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Undermine a corner so a building sinks and leans, come up through the floor of a vault, bury an Animal Control van. The litter instinct as shovel and weapon.

tools_and_powers.name: Pounce (always lands on its feet)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Innate. Charged leap up to 12 m high and 30 m long, with an air-slam on landing. There is never fall damage: impact energy scales with the height fallen. 10 m cracks a road slab; 100 m (a tower top) makes an 8 m crater and a shockwave; the 350 m re-drop from the void makes a 15 m crater.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Height, cliffs, launch geysers and even falling off the world all become ammunition.

tools_and_powers.name: Yowl
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Innate. A cone of sound 40 m long. Hold and slide the pitch: high shatters glass and china across a whole facade at range; middle folds Residents into boxes and sets off every car alarm; low shoves masonry and vehicles at close range. Passes through living things as a ripple of leaves.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Tuning the note to the material makes sound a skill. The full-facade glass sweep is the most satisfying noise in the game.

tools_and_powers.name: Purr
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found in the turbine hall at Stillwater Dam. Sit and purr into whatever you are touching. Match the structure's own wobble (felt as controller rumble, seen as sway) and the vibration builds for 5 to 15 seconds until the joints fatigue and the building shakes itself apart. In soil it liquefies a 15 m circle so cars and footings sink; in bedrock it opens cracks so claws can dig.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: The slowest, funniest and most powerful tool: demolition by contentment. A skyscraper coming apart under a cat that is visibly having a lovely time.

tools_and_powers.name: Loaf
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found in the bakery oven on Sardine Row. Tuck the paws in and Rophe weighs about 90 tonnes. Anything that cannot carry that gives way: sink through a building floor by floor and stop on any storey, crush a car by sitting on it, snap a bridge from mid-span. A loaf cannot be moved: nets, cranes, floods and bulldozers fail.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: It uses the game's real load rules, so it teaches how structures stand while being a pure sight gag: the cat sat on it, so it broke.

tools_and_powers.name: Zoomies
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found in the school gym on Pleasant Loop. Costs 25 Mischief: 8 seconds at 26 m/s with wall and ceiling running. At this speed Rophe goes straight through glass, plasterboard, fences and thin timber, leaving cat-shaped holes; the wake trips alarms and tips Residents over. Chains into Pounce as a horizontal cannonball.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Traversal that is also destruction: the 3 a.m. hallway sprint at city scale, a whole office floor crossed in a straight line through every partition.

tools_and_powers.name: Hairball
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found in the hair salon at the Galleria. A lobbed sticky wad. Where it lands it fuses every loose piece within 2.5 m (up to 60) into one rigid lump and glues that lump to whatever it touched, with the strength of brick mortar. Water dissolves it.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: The building verb that makes every breaking verb bigger: glue a wrecking ball onto a Yarn line, stick a car to the monorail, plug a hydrant until the main bursts, make a ramp out of rubble.

tools_and_powers.name: Static
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found on the doormat of the Cannery Quay substation. Rub against carpet, fabric or Residents' legs to store three levels of charge, then release an arc that jumps between metal objects, 12 m per hop for up to 9 hops. It trips transformers (district blackout), lights gas and fuel, pops airbags and alarms, sets off Clockwork Mice and electrifies standing water, which shorts everything in it and bothers no animal.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Replaces the generic fireball with an ignition source that has rules. You do not shoot fire; you find the path that leads the spark to the fuel.

tools_and_powers.name: Red Dot
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found at the Belvedere observatory. The dot every cat chases now obeys the cat. Paint a line up to 40 m long on any man-made surface, release, and a clean cut 30 m deep follows the line through everything man-made behind it (half a second for glass, 4 seconds for steel). Cut pieces are held by friction and gravity alone. The cut bends around living things.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: The precision tool. Draw one diagonal across a tower and watch the top slide off; cut a door into a vault; slice a ship in half at the waterline.

tools_and_powers.name: Clockwork Mice
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found in the toy shop at the Galleria. Release up to 9 wind-up mice. Each scurries to the nearest load-bearing element and clamps on (Cat's Eye shows which). Then meow: the rhythm of your taps becomes the firing sequence, with gaps from 0.1 to 2 seconds. One mouse cuts one reinforced-concrete column.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Controlled demolition with a musical trigger. The mice find the columns for you, so they quietly teach how buildings stand, and a well-timed nine-beat implosion is a show.

tools_and_powers.name: Table Rule
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found in the rooftop restaurant on Prospect Square. Costs 40 Mischief. For 6 seconds, inside a 30 m sphere, down is wherever you point. Sideways: everything loose falls along the street and structures take their full weight from the side, which most masonry cannot. Up: everything rises, then drops. Plants and animals ignore it; birds stay on the wire.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: The world is a table and you are tipping it. One use empties a car park into the building next door.

tools_and_powers.name: Catgrass (seeds, and a climbing aid)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: First seeds found in the Palm House, more from every freed Giant; carry 9. Spit a seed onto any man-made surface. Oak seed: in 4 seconds a trunk 1.5 m thick rises 25 m, lifting and splitting whatever is above it. Ivy seed: covers 15 by 15 m of wall in 10 seconds, weakens every joint under it to a third and stays as a permanent climbing net. Reed seed: a bed that soaks up flood water and stops fire. Whatever grows is permanent and untouchable, so place it with intent.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: The nature rule turned into your biggest lever: an unbreakable object you can grow on demand inside a building. Every use leaves the map greener.

tools_and_powers.name: Puff Up
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found in the big-cat house at the zoo. Costs a full Mischief ring. The startled-cat fluff taken literally: 15 times size for 20 seconds (4.5 m at the shoulder, about 15 tonnes). Walk through houses, swat buses, sit on a four-storey block. Every other tool scales with you. The camera pulls back to 25 m. Not usable underground.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Kaiju cat. It is the trailer shot, the thumbnail and the reward for a great chain reaction.

tools_and_powers.name: Slow Blink (slow motion)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found at the clockmaker's under the Clock Tower. Hold: the world runs at 12 percent speed, the cat at 60 percent. Costs 1 time pip per 5 seconds. Living things keep normal speed.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: For aiming and for savouring. Pigeons crossing a slow-motion collapse at full speed looks like nothing else.

tools_and_powers.name: Stare (time freeze)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found at the aquarium. Cats stare at things that are not there; now everything man-made stops for up to 8 seconds (1 pip per 2 seconds). Frozen debris is solid: use it as stairs. Swat frozen things to bank impulses, shown as stacked red arrows and released together. Re-position frozen pieces with Scruff.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Sculpting an explosion in mid-air, lining up bank shots through a frozen collapse, running up a staircase of falling cars.

tools_and_powers.name: Take-Back (rewind)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found in the bell chamber of the Clock Tower. World rewind of 10 to 19 seconds for everything man-made within 160 m, while the cat stays free and living things and water carry on. Double-tap for Snap-back, which returns only the cat to where it stood 5 seconds ago. Full rules under time_rewind.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Break the same landmark five different ways without a loading screen, and ride a tower back up into the sky as it un-falls.

tools_and_powers.name: Encore (replay)
tools_and_powers.what_it_does: Found in the old cinema on Sardine Row. The last 60 seconds are always on record. Pause into a free camera with scrub, speed, focus and three filters (Brochure, Model-board, Field Sketch), save postcards, and press Do It Again to Take-Back to the start of the clip if it is still inside the rewind window.
tools_and_powers.why_fun: Every collapse becomes something to show someone. It is also the cheapest marketing the game will ever get.

concept_world.time_rewind:
Name: Take-Back. Rule in one line: it takes back what humans made, and nothing else.

What rewinds: every man-made body and fragment within 160 m (position, spin, damage, burning), every fracture and joint break, collapses, craters and tunnels in the ground, vehicles, Residents (boxes unfold), The Management's units, and the score ledger.

What never rewinds: Rophe (you stay where you are and keep moving at normal speed while the world runs backwards), animals, plants and anything that has grown, and water (you can un-break the dam; you cannot un-spill the reservoir). This is the nature rule applied to time, and it also removes the two hardest technical cases.

Controls: hold to scrub backwards, release to resume; analog speed from 1x to 4x. A red-pencil arc on the HUD shows the seconds available. Double-tap instead for Snap-back: only the cat returns to where it stood 5 seconds ago (the prototype's player-only rewind, kept as a recovery move).

Window: 10 seconds, plus 1 second for each of the 9 lease Clauses found (maximum 19). History is recorded 20 times a second for up to 2,500 objects plus a journal of events. On a truly enormous collapse the window visibly shortens instead of failing. History is wiped by a nap, a void fall or loading a save.

Cost: the time family shares 9 pips (nine lives). Take-Back costs 1 pip per 2 seconds rewound, Snap-back 1 pip. Pips return at 1 per 15 seconds; a nap restores all 9.

On release: time runs forward from that instant with live physics. It is not a recording, so the tower never falls the same way twice.

Three things it is for:
1. Encore destruction: break the same landmark again from another angle with another tool, without loading.
2. Ride the rewind: debris moving backwards is solid. Stand on the rubble, hold Take-Back and the tower carries you up as it reassembles under your paws; let go at the top and push it the other way.
3. Grow, then take back: plant a Catgrass oak in the wreck, rewind the building, and it reassembles around a tree that will not move, already split.

Fairness: taken-back destruction is un-counted (Rollback percent, damages, chain links). Field Notes already earned are kept.

Presentation: debris retraces its path along red-pencil ghost lines; audio plays backwards over the sound of paper un-crumpling; every clock in town runs backwards; the PA says: 'Please disregard the previous notice.'

The rest of the family obeys the same law. Slow Blink (world at 12 percent, cat at 60 percent) and Stare (world frozen for up to 8 seconds) do not apply to living things, so birds fly at full speed through a frozen explosion. Encore keeps the last 60 seconds for replay with a free camera.
concept_world.npcs:
HUMANS: THE RESIDENTS (staging, not people)
- Look: render people, the too-perfect figures from property brochures. 12 faces, 40 outfits, name badges with unit numbers. They speak a friendly made-up murmur with optional subtitles in brochure language ('Have you seen the amenities?').
- Behaviour: each runs a daily loop: commute, cafe, jog, shop, the 14:00 wedding, the endless barbecue, a coach tour of buyers who never buy.
- Drift with the acts. Act I: denial; they step around craters and remark on the weather. Act II: they startle, film you, flee, form a neighbourhood watch armed with laundry baskets, and set out cucumbers (which make the cat jump 3 m straight up: a trap that is also a free launch pad). A few start leaving tuna at a growing shrine. A man with a sandwich board: THE END IS MEOW. Act III: replacements arrive as cheaper copies, with fewer polygons, on wheeled mannequin bases, speech reduced to '[GREETING_03]!'. Act IV: the last few have walked off their loops and sit by the pond with the ducks; they no longer run from you.
- Being harmed: hit hard, a Resident tumbles through the air for the comedy and on landing folds flat with a fwip-thunk into a cardboard box with a carry handle, printed RESIDENT (1) - SOME ASSEMBLY REQUIRED. No blood, no bodies, no sounds of pain. The box is a physics prop: stack boxes to climb, throw them, glue them. A Re-staging van collects boxes and unfolds them at the Sales Office; wreck the van and the boxes pile up. Dogs keep walking, towing their owner's box on the lead.
- The Management's staff are Residents in hi-vis: Tidy Crews (Act I); Animal Control with nets, carriers, laser-dot decoys, sprinklers and robot vacuums (Act II); Public Works with water cannon, bulldozers and a net helicopter (Act III). None can hurt you. Capture means a carrier ride to the Pound across the map, which is full of cages to open and is itself demolishable: fast travel with a punchline. An 'Unsupervised' toggle switches enforcement off entirely.
- The exception: the Surveyor at Lot 000 is AS IS. He gardens, whistles, puts out a saucer and writes the margin notes. If no exception to 'humans can be harmed' is wanted, replace him with an empty bench holding his hat, thermos and field journal; the ending still works.

ANIMALS (real, AS IS; about 20 species, chosen by which good free rigs exist)
- Town: pigeons, crows, gulls, dogs, the cat colony, squirrels, rats. Park and water: ducks, a heron, koi. Hills and edge: deer, foxes, rabbits, cows, sheep, horses. Underground: moles, bats. Zoo: an elephant, giraffes, penguins, flamingos.
- Core behaviour: unbothered. They never panic at destruction, never get hurt and never play a pain reaction. An animal on the ground stays exactly where it has decided to be, and solid things lose. An animal in the air is never struck; flocks open and close around debris. If their footing collapses they ride the biggest piece down and step off at the bottom. The one thing that makes a flock take off is the cat running at it, which is how a player clears a line of fire, and is also simply what cats do.
- They are useful: crows circle over Treats; moles lead to Giants; rats know the sewers; the cat colony answers a rally call and swats everything off every surface in a shop; dogs chase you only if you hiss at them or steal their ball; a freed elephant can be ridden and walks through walls because nothing can stop it.
- They are the progress you can feel: wildlife follows Returned ground. Birds nest in ruins, deer graze in the car park, fish move into flooded basements.

TREATMENT CHOSEN, AND THE ALTERNATIVES
- Chosen: flat-pack. Funny, instantly readable, no gore, produces a useful physics object, fits the showroom fiction and keeps a low age rating within reach.
- Rejected: realistic injury or gore (wrong tone, rating and store risk, turns the cat into a monster).
- Rejected: invulnerable humans who only run (the brief wants humans harmable, and it would blur what makes animals special).
- Rejected: generic knock-out with stars, or silent despawn (forgettable, and despawning breaks the promise that nothing vanishes).
concept_world.nature_rule:
THE LAW (three sentences the whole game obeys)
Living things cannot be broken, burned, drowned, crushed, moved against their will or edited. Solid things break on them or go around them. Energy passes through them.

IN-FICTION REASON
Plants and animals are the Survey: original, real records filed AS IS underneath the lease, which no tenant, no rollback and no time power may alter. Clause 4 of the lease says so: WILDLIFE AS IS. The cat is covered by the same clause, which is why the cat cannot die.

HOW IT LOOKS (one effect, learned once)
Whenever force meets life: a row of red dots appears under the plant or animal with the proofreader's word 'stet' (let it stand), its sepia field-sketch outline flashes for a quarter of a second, and a soft wooden tock plays. No HUD message, no shield bubble, no scolding. The aiming reticle shows the dots before you fire, so nothing is wasted by surprise. (This replaces the prototype's green bubble and 'NATURE IS PROTECTED' alert.)

CASE BY CASE
- Debris and thrown objects: trunks, main boughs and any animal standing on the ground are anvils, whatever their size. A car wraps around an oak; a bus folds around a pigeon; a tower falling on a grove is combed into strips by the trunks. Foliage is soft: small pieces pass through, slow down, and some lodge there (trees collect trophies: a shopping trolley 15 m up). Birds in flight are never struck; the flock parts. Projectiles ricochet off trunks and standing animals with no loss of energy, so a miss becomes a bank shot.
- Fire: burns everything man-made and cannot burn life. A flame front reaching plants turns into a wave of blossom in flame colours and stops there. Hedges and tree lines are firebreaks you can read and plan with.
- Floods: plants stand in the flow and make eddies that trap floating debris into dams. Land animals step onto floating wreckage or swim calmly; ducks and fish arrive. Flooded ground regrows three times faster.
- Explosions and Yowl: the blast passes straight through life (a ripple of leaves, ruffled feathers) and hits what is behind it. A tree never shields a building from a shockwave.
- Gravity and time powers: do not apply to life. In Table Rule cars fall sideways and birds stay on the wire. In Slow Blink and Stare, animals and wind in the leaves keep full speed.
- Potted and indoor plants: the pot is man-made. When it breaks, the plant lands upright, roots where it lands and grows to full size in 30 seconds. Every houseplant you free becomes a tree.
- Underground: roots cannot be cut. Tunnels bend around them, and they hold tunnels up.

THE RULE AS A FEATURE
1. Rewilding is the win condition. Progress is not rubble; it is what grows where the town was. The more you destroy, the more beautiful the map becomes, and the stars come out as the grid dies.
2. Catgrass: you plant untouchable growth as a demolition tool: an oak erupting through 20 floors, ivy that pries a facade off and leaves a permanent ladder, a reed bed that drinks a flood.
3. Suppressed Giants: 40 heritage trees are pinned under specific buildings (sepia ghosts in Cat's Eye). Clear the footprint and the Giant returns through whatever is still above it.
4. Anvils and billiards: unbreakable trunks are fixed anchors for Yarn slingshots and tripwires, cheese-wires for falling towers and cushions for ricochet shots.
5. Sanctuary: no Management unit may operate within 6 m of an animal. A flock of sheep is a moving safe zone; a net passes harmlessly over a cat sitting among pigeons.
6. Liberation: the zoo, aquarium and Palm House are all cage and no victim. Breaking them is pure release.
7. Spectacle: full-speed birds crossing a frozen collapse is an image no other destruction game has.

WHY IT WILL NOT FRUSTRATE
Life never eats a shot (it passes through, ricochets, or you shoo the flock by running at it), never blocks a blast, never has to be cleared for progress (the 85 percent rule counts only man-made mass), and is never dense exactly where a landmark needs to fall unless that collision is the joke. The park is designed as the place you go to do nothing.
concept_world.progression_and_goals:
No quests, no XP, no currency, no crafting, no map covered in icons, no checklist on the HUD. Structure comes from the world.

1. Rollback percent. Per district: the share of original man-made standing mass no longer standing, shown in the world on the district's property price board (FROM 450,000 ... FROM 12 ... FREE TO GOOD HOME ... RETURNED). At 85 percent the district is Returned and The Management writes off the rest, which peels and overgrows automatically. Nobody hunts for the last lamp post.
2. Acts. Global percent moves the whole map through four acts (15, 40, 70, 100), each changing enforcement, Residents, music, sky and how fast things fall. The finale starts when 6 of 8 districts are Returned: what is left of the Sales Tower gets up and runs for the edge.
3. Treats, 15 of them: the powers. Five verbs are yours after the intro (Paw, Claws Out, Pounce, Yowl, Dig). The rest sit in plain sight on landmarks, marked by circling crows, reachable in any order, most within the first 3 hours. Powers are never bought.
4. Clauses, 9 of them: the story. Each is one short paragraph of the lease with a handwritten margin note, hidden at the heart of a set-piece: PREMISES AS FOUND (Clock Tower bell chamber), FIXTURES AS INSTALLED (Galleria strongroom), OCCUPANTS AS STAGED (Showhome No. 1, a wardrobe of folded Residents), WILDLIFE AS IS (zoo office), UTILITIES AS METERED (substation), VIEWS AS ADVERTISED (observatory), WATER AS BORROWED (dam gallery), GROUND AS GIVEN (the underside of the world), TERM AS EXPIRED (tower penthouse safe). Each adds 1 second to Take-Back; all 9 open the secret ending.
5. Giants, 40 of them: events, not pick-ups. Each freed Giant is a building-wrecking eruption and yields Catgrass seeds.
6. Field Notes, 120 of them: the Surveyor's sketchbook fills in when you do something worth drawing ('Fig. 14: subject loafs on bank. Bank fails.' 'Fig. 31: omnibus halted by pigeon.' 'Fig. 77: subject exits planet from below.'). Silhouettes of unfilled pages work as hints. A subset are the Steam achievements.
7. Records: heaviest single collapse, longest chain, highest fall, most Residents boxed by one swat. Local first, friends leaderboards later.
8. Whims: when Rophe idles near an opportunity one dry line appears ('That vase is very close to the edge.'). No reward but Mischief. They are tone, not tasks.

Is there an ending? Yes, three (see story), reached in roughly 8 to 12 hours, and the sandbox continues after any of them.

Two modes on the main menu from the first launch, nothing gated:
- The Lease: everything above.
- Toybox: all 20 tools, all districts, enforcement off unless wanted, time-of-day and season sliders, a spawn menu, instant re-stage of any district. For pure-chaos players and for people making videos.

After the ending: re-stage into Lease 2, 3, 4. Each lease advances the season (spring, summer, autumn, winter with snow and a frozen bay), everything that grew last time is still there with the town rebuilt around it, and optional mutators unlock (low gravity, everything is glass, giant Residents).
concept_world.save_system:
Yes: save everything, automatically, permanently. A destruction game that forgets on the next launch is a toy; one that remembers is a place.

What is saved: the world as differences from the brochure-fresh map, in 64 m regions: which elements are broken, every settled chunk (type, position, rotation: about 20 bytes each), all ground edits and rubble (compressed), everything that has grown, water levels, boxes, vehicles; plus the global ledger (Rollback, act, tools, Clauses, Field Notes, records, time of day, season). Moving debris is settled first; fires are saved as burnt, not burning. Target size: 20-60 MB typically, under 150 MB for a fully wrecked map.

How:
- Autosave, invisible. Every 60 seconds only the regions that changed are written on a background thread; also on quit, on entering the void and when a district is Returned. Writes are atomic (temporary file, then rename) with 3 rotating backups, so a crash or power cut never costs more than a minute.
- Nap to save, the manual save inside the fiction. Curl up in any sunbeam, any box, or on the bench at Lot 000. The game takes a named Snapshot, refills the 9 time pips and plays a 10-second time-lapse to the next dawn, in which the district greens and The Management re-stages its cardboard.
- 3 save slots called Leases, each with 9 Snapshots (nine lives), each Snapshot with an automatic postcard thumbnail. Load any Snapshot from the pause menu.
- Steam Cloud through Steam's automatic file sync, which needs configuration but no code; on itch.io saves are local with an export button.
- A version number in every file and a migration step, because saves must survive patches.

Reset the simulation, inside the fiction: the Sales Office lobby holds a 4 m table-top scale model of the whole town (1:400) that mirrors the real one live; wrecked blocks are wrecked on the model. It is the reset interface, and it is also a toy: swat a miniature tower and the real one outside the window comes down.
- Re-stage a district: flip that district's plate on the model. Its buildings return; what grew there stays, and returning walls re-form already split around trees. Other districts are untouched.
- Re-stage everything: sit in the middle of the model for 3 seconds. An automatic Snapshot is taken first, so no world is ever lost by accident. The Management says: 'Thank you for renewing.' A new lease and season begin.
- Brochure-fresh world: start a new Lease slot.
What always carries over within a slot: tools, Clauses, Field Notes, records, cosmetics, lease count and every living thing that has grown. Nature only ratchets forward.

Also: export a wrecked world as one file (a Ruin) to send to a friend, who can walk through your valley and keep wrecking it.
concept_world.art_and_audio_direction:
ART
- Three looks in sequence, which is the game's visual story: Brochure (spotless, golden hour, saturated, shallow depth of field), Ruin (raw concrete, rebar, hanging dust, hazard tape, tarp blue), Wild (white paper buildings in a green valley under real weather and a sky full of stars). Screenshots from hour 1 and hour 10 should look like two different games on the same streets.
- Three hands for the simulation layer, never mixed. Print: plotter blue on white, for The Management (notices, plans, labels on man-made things). Ink: sepia handwriting and watercolour, for the Survey (labels on living things, margin notes). Red Pencil: vermilion, slightly wobbling, for Rophe's powers (delete loop on a grabbed object, 'stet' dots under life, the transpose curve, a caret where a seed is planted, arrows for banked impulses). Glitches are print errors, not screen errors: colour plates out of register, peeling sheets, paper jams that concertina an object, crop marks in the sky. Banned: green code rain, black void, scan lines, pixel sorting, anything that reads as a monitor.
- The cat is the hero asset and gets the most care: shell-fur shader, dust and wet states (dark fur shows white dust beautifully; the cat shakes and grooms it off), a procedural spine, tail, ears and foot placement over a small set of authored cycles, big readable eyes, and the signature head turn toward the nearest witness.
- Animals are the most natural-moving things in the world; Residents are deliberately a little stiff. That contrast is the fiction.
- One house material library (about 12 master materials built from CC0 PBR textures) is applied to every imported model by the asset pipeline. Sources: Kenney, Quaternius, Poly Haven and ambientCG (CC0) first; then Sketchfab, itch.io and OpenGameArt filtered to CC0 or CC-BY, logged in a credits manifest; museum open-access scans for the fossil. Nothing with non-commercial or no-derivatives terms, nothing ripped from other games.
- Rendering: move the project from GL Compatibility to Forward+ with real-time global illumination, volumetric fog and dust, reflections on wet streets; 1080p at 60 fps on the RTX 5070, with a Destruction Quality slider that scales debris budgets on weaker machines.
- Camera: low, cat-height third person; pulls back automatically with the size of what is falling; first-person whisker-cam in tunnels; shake is capped by a player setting.
- HUD: one ring (Mischief), nine pips (time), a radial tool wheel. Everything else is in the world: price boards, notices, labels.

AUDIO (half of AAA feel is sound)
- Destruction is layered per material and size: crack, body, debris tail, sub-bass thump, dust hiss. Distant events arrive late and muffled; interiors ring; tunnels close in.
- Music starts inside the world: The Management pipes showroom bossa-nova muzak through street speakers. Destroy the speakers or trip the power and it dies in that district. As Rollback rises the muzak warps, skips and loops, and an acoustic theme (hand percussion, upright bass, cello, kalimba) grows in its place, with brush-drum jazz breaks for Zoomies. Returned districts have no music at all: wind, water, birds, insects. The soundscape rewilds with the map.
- The simulation never bleeps. Its sounds are paper: tearing, crumpling, pencil scratch, plotter servo, the rubber-stamp thunk of every notice.
- Voices: no recorded dialogue. Residents and the PA use synthesised friendly gibberish with subtitles. The cat has a real, varied voice set (meow, chirp, trill, yowl, purr), and the controller purrs when Rophe does.
- Sources: CC0 and royalty-free libraries plus the Python sound generator already in the project; every file logged with its licence.
signature_moments: The First Glass: one wine glass slides off the bar in slow motion; sixty seconds later the front of the bar is in the street.
The Pigeon and the Bus: a city bus doing 50 km/h folds itself around a pigeon that does not look up.
Loaf on the Bank: Rophe tucks in on the roof and sinks, purring, through twelve floors one at a time into the vault.
Ride the Rewind: standing on the rubble of a tower, hold Take-Back and be carried 80 m into the air as it reassembles under your paws; then push it the other way.
The Scale Model: in the Sales Office lobby, swat a 20 cm tower off the architect's model and watch the real one across the square come down a heartbeat later.
The Mirror at the Edge: the tag over your own head reads ROPHE AS CAT; a red pencil swaps the words; the title was a line of the world's code all along.
Facade Dominoes: one swat in Phase 2 and forty house-fronts fall in a row into the white.
Through the Planet: dig past three buried older versions of the town, flood the assumed magma, break the last sheet, fall out of the bottom of the world and come back through the sky as a meteor.
The Dam: the breach, 70 seconds of flood wave down the whole river corridor, then the drained reservoir revealing a drowned grove still standing, and a day of rain.
Purr the Tower: find the resonance; 2,000 panes shed like scales and a skyscraper shakes itself apart under a contented cat.
The Zoo Break: an elephant strolls, unhurried, through a collapsing glass mall with Rophe riding on its head.
The Giant: clear a lobby floor and a 60 m oak comes back up through twenty storeys, wearing the building like a broken bracelet.
The China Shop: Slow Blink through 4,000 pieces of porcelain while sparrows cross the frame at full speed.
The Ferris Wheel: cut loose, it rolls the length of the boardwalk into the cannery, and the fireworks barge answers.
Rain of Your Own Garbage: throw a bus off the east edge; twenty seconds later it falls out of the sky onto Downtown.

The Walking Tower: what is left of the Sales Tower stands up on crane legs and makes for the edge with the lease; take it apart on the move. If it reaches the edge it falls and is dropped back like everything else.
Stars: trip the last substation at night and the Milky Way switches on over a dark, green valley.
The Lap: the tag is corrected to CAT AS CAT and marked 'stet'; press one button to curl up on the Surveyor's knee.
extra_ideas: Cat's Eye view: night vision plus AS labels plus a structural X-ray (load-bearing parts, materials, buried mains, ghost Giants). It is the planning tool, the lore reader and an accessibility aid in one; about 600 two-word label jokes carry the world-building.

Progress shown in the world instead of menus: property price boards per district, radio adverts rewritten after you hit something ('now with open-plan living'), a tour guide who keeps describing landmarks that are gone, an insurance adjuster with a clipboard and a running damages total.

The Open House: every day at 09:00 a coach of prospective buyers arrives and never buys. It is a daily moving set-piece and the clock by which The Management re-stages its cardboard, so a wrecked district always has something new to knock over.
Light pollution as a mechanic: the number of stars scales with how much of the power grid is dead.

More cat verbs for later updates: If I Fits (hide in any box, bin or washing machine and pop out of any other container within 150 m), Liquid Cat (pour through any 10 cm gap or pipe), Biscuits (knead a surface until concrete goes soft and sags).

Hats and collars as cosmetics found in shops, including the prototype's wizard hat; in Toybox the wizard hat turns Static into fireballs as a nod to the first build. At the CAT AS CAT ending the Surveyor offers a collar tag reading ROPHE.

Sharing built in: recording-timeline markers on every landmark collapse, a one-button postcard mode with brochure frames, and automatic before-and-after postcards of each district from the same camera spot.
Free demo = Sardine Row only (one district, six tools, the edge visible but walled off by hoardings reading COMING SOON). It is the same build as the vertical slice.

Store presentation: title lockup CAT AS ROPHE with the subtitle 'a catastrophe sandbox' so the pun lands and the word catastrophe is searchable; capsule art = dark cat, white paper city, one red pencil stroke.

Comfort and accessibility: Unsupervised toggle (no enforcement), limits for camera shake and flashes, hold-or-toggle for every input, colour-blind-safe label colours, subtitles for the babble, a one-handed tool wheel.

Blank Page mode (reward for the secret ending, later update): an empty slab where the player stages a small town from collected props and buildings, wrecks it and shares it as a file; the natural path to Workshop support.
Second cat: drop-in local co-op kitten with the same rules and a shared Mischief ring, once the single-player build is solid.
Seasons as lease variants: autumn leaf fall, winter snow load on roofs and a frozen bay that can be cracked.
Other Lots glimpsed in the Margin (alpine resort, reef marina) are the expansion and sequel hook, already inside the fiction.
risks: Scope against a one-agent, zero-budget production. AAA feel in every respect across 8 districts is not reachable in one pass. Mitigation: one vertical slice to final quality first; ship districts one at a time (Early Access); fix the cut order in advance: walking tower, Puff Up, large zoo animals, flood simulation, seasons.

The cat's animation. The player looks at Rophe for the whole game and there is no animator; a stiff cat sinks the AAA impression faster than anything else. Mitigation: best available free rig, a heavy procedural layer, and treat this as the first milestone, not the last.

Physics load in GDScript. Thousands of bodies plus support checks can sink the frame rate. Mitigation: Jolt, pooled bodies, batched drawing of settled debris, hard budgets (2,000 moving, 250 new per frame), time-sliced structure checks, a Destruction Quality slider.

Voxel ground without native code. Meshing 0.5 m cells in script is slow. Mitigation: generate only where dug, 16 m chunks on worker threads; evaluate a prebuilt voxel extension only if it supports this exact engine version; fallback is fixed dig sites instead of dig-anywhere.

World rewind is the hardest feature. Mitigation: the rule that life and water never rewind removes the worst cases; build it in tiers (bodies, then fractures, then ground); the window shortens under load instead of breaking.

Water. Real fluid simulation is a trap. Mitigation: a coarse flood height map on a 2 m grid and simple volume filling for tunnels, fed only from authored sources (dam, water tower, mains, aquifer, sea).

Asset licences and cohesion. Free models vary in quality and terms, and most cannot be fractured as they are. Mitigation: CC0 first, a licence manifest from day one, the house material library, element-kit buildings, and the Changelog fiction that makes older styles belong underground.

Harming humans. Even bloodless, tumbling realistic people can read badly and affect age ratings. Mitigation: stylised render people, flat-pack boxes, no pain audio, and early outside playtests of exactly this.
The nature rule as an irritation. Mitigation: pass-through, ricochet, preview and shoo rules; watch playtests for any moment a player says the tree was in the way and redesign that spot.

Will a paper-and-proofmarks identity read as a simulation? It is original but less literal than code on a screen. Mitigation: AS labels, loops, placeholders and names like LOOP_03 do the explaining; test the edge with fresh players and add more literal process language if they say drawing instead of simulation.
The AS wordplay is English-only. Mitigation: labels stay in English in every language, as code does, with an optional translated gloss; notices and margin notes are translated normally.
Sandbox emptiness once everything is down. Mitigation: daily cardboard re-staging, Take-Back, district re-stage, leases and seasons, Toybox.
The single unbreakable human bends the rule that humans can be harmed. It is flagged, optional, and has a no-exception fallback (the empty bench).
Save size and compatibility across updates. Mitigation: region differences, versioned files, migration tests run in the headless build.
Tone drift toward mean-spirited or twee. The test for every joke: is it something a cat would do, and does The Management stay polite?

sources.name: Kenney (kenney.nl)
sources.covers: Low-poly kits: buildings (commercial, suburban, industrial, modular, interior-capable), roads and street furniture, cars, trains/trams, boats, factory machinery, furniture, food/shop goods, nature. About 50 3D packs.
sources.license: CC0 1.0 on every pack page; kenney.nl/support: public domain, commercial use allowed, attribution not required. Only ask: do not use the Kenney logo on its own.
sources.automation: Yes, scriptable without login (checked 2026-11-13). Static .zip URLs are gone: each pack page has data-download-id = hex of 'assets/<slug>'. GET https://kenney.nl/download-link/<hex> returns JSON {url: https://kenney.nl/download/<hex>/<signature>?expires=<ts>}; then GET that URL. The JSON step worked with no cookies; the zip step was not executed.
sources.formats: One zip per kit: GLB/glTF, FBX, OBJ plus a shared palette PNG (formats are not listed on the pages; from memory).
sources.style: Clean flat-colour low-poly, hard edges, toy-like proportions, one palette texture per kit.

sources.name: OpenGameArt
sources.covers: Community archive of 2D/3D art; mirrors of Kenney and Quaternius packs plus many older low-poly props, buildings and vehicles.
sources.license: Per asset: CC0, CC BY 3.0/4.0, CC BY-SA 3.0/4.0, OGA-BY 3.0, GPL 2/3, LGPL (from memory; site returned HTTP 403 today).

sources.formats: Varies: .blend, OBJ, FBX, DAE.
sources.style: Very mixed; 3D section is largely dated.
sources.best_items: Nothing verified this session. Treat as fallback only; restrict searches to CC0 and OGA-BY.
sources.caveats: Avoid GPL and CC BY-SA art in a closed commercial build. CC BY 3.0 and BY-SA 3.0 forbid adding technological restrictions, which OGA itself flags as a concern for DRM-wrapped stores; OGA-BY removes that clause. Quality control is minimal.

sources.name: Sketchfab (downloadable CC0 / CC BY)
sources.covers: Largest general model host. CC BY pool has realistic cranes, buildings, street props and vehicles of very uneven quality; CC0 pool is mostly museum photogrammetry.
sources.license: Per model (from api.sketchfab.com/v3/licenses): CC0, CC BY 4.0, CC BY-SA, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC, BY-NC-SA, BY-NC-ND, Free Standard, Standard, Editorial. Only CC0 and CC BY are safe for a game that modifies assets.
sources.automation: Search and metadata are public without auth: https://api.sketchfab.com/v3/search?type=models&downloadable=true&license=cc0|by&q=<kw>&sort_by=-likeCount and /v3/models/<uid> (licence, faceCount, tags). Download endpoint /v3/models/<uid>/download returned 401 without credentials: needs a user account and API token.
sources.formats: Auto-converted glTF/GLB/USDZ plus the original upload.
sources.style: Anything; mostly realistic PBR among the useful CC BY items.
sources.best_items: URL pattern https://sketchfab.com/models/<uid>. 'Tower Crane' by Chamodp, CC BY 4.0, 32,308 faces, 2K textures, tags gameready/noai: 49851dc7a51b43bda6aea06856c26a85 | 'Tower crane KB-674' by Randonavt, CC BY, 33,220 faces: 0667cfae11e44969978ab28eea512d84 | 'Tower crane KB-160' by Randonavt, CC BY, 23,064 faces, separated parts: b473c900833648ee937646989f4e00a4 | 'Abandoned street lights pack' by sergeilihandristov, CC BY, 22,315 faces: c853eca300e8435d8fe9206bcb524eda | 'CCity Building Set 1' by neberkenezer, CC BY, 18,372 faces: a2d5c7bfcc2148fb8994864c43dfcc97. Use only as single hero props for gaps, not as a base library.
sources.caveats: Licences are self-declared: game rips, branded vehicles and AI-generated meshes appear under CC BY/CC0. CC0 searches for building/car/street returned almost only museum scans (100K-1.9M faces). Popular 'modular city' hits are Free Standard, not CC (e.g. 'Neighbourhood City Modular lowpoly', 'Full Gameready City Buildings IV [HongKong]'). Fresh bulk CC0 uploads (e.g. October 2026 military helicopters, 137-190K faces) need provenance checks.

top_picks.item: Quaternius - Downtown City MegaKit (free Standard tier, 153 assets)
top_picks.use_for: Hero downtown blocks: modular Boston/NYC facades, doors, windows, fire escapes, street and road pieces.
top_picks.why: Newest (May 2026) and most detailed free modular city kit at human scale; glTF. Break per module; facades are shells, so put a procedural solid core behind them.

top_picks.item: Kenney - Modular Buildings v2.1 (100 pieces)

top_picks.why: Modular pieces are natural fracture units; scriptable download.
